name: The Melian obsidian trade

claims.text: Melian obsidian reached the Greek mainland by c. 11,000 BC.
Obsidian can be chemically traced to its source volcano.
Its presence at Franchthi Cave demonstrates open-water voyaging.
Melian obsidian was traded alongside other materials, showing an established, multi-commodity exchange network rather than a single specialised trade route.

summary: Volcanic glass from the island of Melos was shipped across the Aegean from the Mesolithic onwards — the earliest evidence of seafaring in the region.
significance: The earliest evidence of seafaring in the Mediterranean, thousands of years before farming reached Greece.
body:
From around 11,000 BC, obsidian — volcanic glass used for sharp blades — was carried from the island of Melos across the Aegean.

Obsidian from Melos was found in the Franchthi Cave in the Argolid in layers dating to around 11,000 BC. Melos is an island and was never connected to the mainland, so someone crossed open water to get it — the earliest hard evidence for sea travel anywhere in the Mediterranean.

Obsidian gives a cutting edge sharper than surgical steel and can be chemically fingerprinted to its source volcano, so its distribution maps ancient exchange with unusual precision. A distribution map cannot tell us whether specialist sailors, direct visitors or repeated hand-to-hand exchanges carried each piece. Melian obsidian nevertheless turns up across the Aegean for eight thousand years.

Sites receiving Melian obsidian also frequently show other non-local materials moving alongside it, from particular pottery styles to marble and metals, suggesting that obsidian exchange was rarely an isolated, single-purpose activity but rather one strand within broader, sustained networks of contact linking Aegean communities across a very long span of prehistory.

name: Height of Cycladic figurine production

claims.text: Cycladic figurines were carved from marble using abrasives rather than metal tools.
They were originally painted, with traces still detectable.
Most were made for funerary deposition.
Extensive looting has destroyed the context of most known examples.
They represent a mother goddess.
Figurines range widely in size, from small handheld pieces to examples approaching or exceeding a metre in height.

summary: The distinctive folded-arm marble figurines of the Cyclades were produced in quantity for burial.
significance: The high point of Early Cycladic culture, whose marble figurines are among the most recognisable objects of the Aegean Bronze Age.
body:
Between about 2800 and 2300 BC, in the Early Bronze Age, the islanders of the Cyclades produced marble figurines in large numbers, mainly for burials.

Carved from local white marble with abrasives — no metal tools were needed — the figurines range from a few centimetres to nearly life size. They were painted: traces of blue and red survive, and "ghosts" of weathered paint show eyes, hair and facial markings on faces we now perceive as blank.

Most cannot stand; the feet point downwards, so they were made to lie down, consistent with burial. Their spare geometry influenced Brancusi, Modigliani and Moore.

Their popularity created a serious problem. Looting to supply the twentieth-century art market destroyed the archaeological context of the great majority, so most known figurines cannot be securely dated or interpreted.

The type also spans a considerable range of scale: most examples fit easily in the hand, but a small number of exceptional figures approach or exceed a metre in height, examples so large and fragile that they must have required real skill and investment to carve and move without breaking, raising the question of what distinguished the graves or contexts that merited such an unusually large offering.

name: Destruction of the House of the Tiles

claims.text: The House of the Tiles was destroyed by fire around 2200 BC.
Numerous Early Helladic II sites were disrupted in the same broad period.
A severe aridification event affected the Near East around 2200 BC.
The destructions were caused by invading Greek speakers.
A tumulus was raised directly over the ruins of the House of the Tiles, suggesting the site retained special significance to those who rebuilt at Lerna afterward.

summary: The monumental administrative building at Lerna burned around 2200 BC, part of a wider disruption across mainland Greece.
significance: Part of a wave of destructions that ended the prosperous Early Bronze Age culture of mainland Greece.
body:
Around 2200 BC the House of the Tiles at Lerna, in the Argolid, was destroyed by fire.

The fire that ended the House of the Tiles is one node in a pattern: many Early Helladic II settlements in the Argolid and beyond were destroyed or abandoned within a few generations around 2200 BC.

Explanations have cycled through invasion by incoming Indo-European speakers, internal conflict, and — currently most favoured — the 4.2 kiloyear climate event, a severe aridification episode documented across the Near East and implicated in the collapse of the Akkadian Empire and Egypt's Old Kingdom at almost the same time.

The fire preserved hundreds of clay sealings, so the destruction is also the reason we know how the building worked.

Rather than simply clearing the ruin and building over it, whoever resettled Lerna afterward chose to raise an earthen tumulus directly over the burned remains of the House of the Tiles, leaving the ground beneath it untouched — a deliberate act of commemoration or avoidance that suggests the destroyed building retained real meaning for the community even after the centralised authority it once represented had disappeared.

name: The first Minoan palaces

claims.text: Palatial complexes appear on Crete from c. 1900 BC.
They combined storage, craft production, administration and ritual functions.
Administrative record-keeping using written scripts accompanied their emergence.
The first palaces were destroyed c. 1700 BC by earthquake.
The palaces lacked substantial defensive fortifications, unlike contemporary centres in the Near East, suggesting relatively low levels of external military threat on Crete.

summary: Around 1900 BC large multi-functional complexes appear at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros — the first states in Europe.
significance: The appearance of the first states in Europe, with palaces, writing and organised economies.
body:
Around 1900 BC the first palaces were built on Crete, at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, and somewhat later at Zakros.

The First Palace period marks a step change: centralised storage on an industrial scale, craft workshops, and administration recorded in Cretan Hieroglyphic and then Linear A. Storage capacity at Knossos alone ran to hundreds of thousands of litres.

Why this happened on Crete and not the mainland is debated. Crete escaped the destructions of c. 2200 BC, sits at the crossing point of Egyptian, Levantine and Aegean routes, and produced surplus oil and wine that reward central storage and redistribution.

All the first palaces were destroyed around 1700 BC, probably by earthquake, and immediately rebuilt on a grander scale.

One striking feature of these early Cretan states is what they did not build: unlike contemporary palace centres in the Near East and, later, the heavily walled Mycenaean citadels on the Greek mainland, the first Minoan palaces had no substantial defensive walls, which most archaeologists take as evidence that Crete's rulers, protected by the sea and perhaps by a genuine absence of serious rivals, simply did not face the kind of sustained military threat that made fortification a priority elsewhere.

name: The Theran eruption

claims.text: The Theran eruption was among the largest volcanic events of the Holocene.
Tsunami deposits associated with the eruption have been identified on Crete.
Radiocarbon and ice-core evidence support a date of c. 1620–1600 BC.
Egyptian archaeological synchronisms support a later date of c. 1500 BC.
The eruption directly caused the collapse of Minoan civilisation.
The eruption inspired Plato's account of Atlantis.
Akrotiri shows no human remains and evidence of advance preparation, suggesting its population evacuated before the final eruption.

summary: One of the largest volcanic eruptions of the last ten thousand years destroyed the island of Thera and buried the town of Akrotiri.
significance: One of the largest volcanic eruptions in human history, which buried Akrotiri and affected the whole eastern Mediterranean.
body:
The volcano of Thera (Santorini), in the southern Cyclades, erupted in the 17th or 16th century BC, probably around 1610 BC.

The eruption ejected an estimated 60 cubic kilometres of material, collapsing the centre of the island into a caldera 12 km across. Ash fell across the eastern Mediterranean and has been identified in cores from the Nile delta to the Black Sea, making it a chronological marker for the whole region.

Tsunamis struck northern Crete; deposits containing marine shells, pottery and animal bone have been found inland at Palaikastro.

The date is a long-running dispute. Radiocarbon dating of an olive branch buried alive in the ash and Greenland ice-core acidity spikes support c. 1620–1600 BC. Egyptian synchronisms from pottery cross-dating suggest c. 1500 BC. A century separates the two, which matters enormously: the high chronology means the eruption cannot have caused the Cretan destructions of 1450 BC.

Notably, excavations at Akrotiri have found no human skeletons and clear signs that residents had already removed their most valuable possessions and blocked doorways before the final explosive phase, implying that warning tremors gave the population time to evacuate — in sharp contrast to Pompeii, which the site is often compared to.

name: The Mycenae shaft graves

claims.text: The Mycenae shaft graves date to c. 1650–1500 BC and contained exceptional gold assemblages.
Grave goods include Baltic amber and Egyptian-influenced imagery.
The burials predate the traditional date of the Trojan War by roughly three centuries.
The wealth derives from Mycenaean mercenary service abroad.
A second, later grave circle (Circle B) found nearby contains comparable but somewhat less spectacular burials.

summary: Six deep shaft graves at Mycenae, used c. 1650–1500 BC, held the richest burials yet found in Bronze Age Europe.
significance: The richest burials of Bronze Age Europe, marking the rise of the first Mycenaean ruling families.
body:
Between about 1650 and 1500 BC the ruling families of Mycenae buried their dead in deep shaft graves, in two grave circles.

Grave Circle A held nineteen bodies with around 15 kg of gold: five funerary masks, gold breastplates, diadems, hundreds of gold discs sewn onto clothing, bronze daggers inlaid with gold and silver hunting scenes, amber from the Baltic, and ostrich eggs from Africa.

The wealth is a puzzle. It appears suddenly, in a society with no preceding tradition of such display. Proposals include Mycenaean mercenaries returning enriched from Egyptian service — the daggers show Nilotic scenes — and control of trade routes.

Schliemann found them in 1876 and identified them with Agamemnon's household. They are roughly three centuries too early. He was wrong about the identification and right that something remarkable was buried there. A second, somewhat earlier and generally less spectacularly furnished grave circle, Circle B, was found nearby decades later, outside the later fortification walls, and is now understood as belonging to the same elite lineage in an earlier phase of its rise to prominence.

name: The Cretan destructions of c. 1450 BC

claims.text: Most Minoan centres outside Knossos were destroyed or abandoned c. 1450 BC.
Knossos continued in use with Linear B administration in Greek.
Warrior burials with mainland weapon types appear on Crete in this phase.
The destructions resulted from Mycenaean conquest.
Some scholars argue for internal Cretan unrest or natural disaster rather than external conquest as an alternative or contributing explanation.

summary: Almost every Minoan centre on Crete was destroyed within a short period; only Knossos continued, thereafter administered in Greek.
significance: The end of the Minoan palace civilisation on Crete and the beginning of Mycenaean Greek rule there.
body:
Around 1450 BC most of the palaces and towns of Minoan Crete were destroyed, many by fire.

Zakros, Phaistos, Malia, Gournia and Ayia Triada were all destroyed or abandoned around 1450 BC, many with evidence of burning. Knossos survived and its administration continued — now writing Linear B, in Greek.

The simplest reading is Mycenaean conquest: a mainland takeover of the island, with Knossos retained as the administrative centre. Supporting evidence includes warrior burials with mainland-style weapons appearing on Crete and the shift in script and language.

The eruption of Thera is too early on the high chronology to be the direct cause, though longer-term economic damage may have weakened Crete beforehand.

Not every scholar accepts conquest as the full explanation. Some point instead to internal social breakdown, earthquake damage, or a combination of factors weakening Minoan palatial authority from within, with the arrival of Mycenaean administrators at Knossos following rather than causing the collapse of the other centres. The debate remains unresolved because the archaeological signature of conquest and of internal collapse can look very similar on the ground.

name: Linear B administration at Knossos

claims.text: Linear B was used at Knossos for palace administration after c. 1450 BC.
Linear B records an early form of Greek.
The tablets survive because fire baked the unfired clay.
The tablets name deities later worshipped in Classical Greece.
Similar Linear B archives were later found on the Greek mainland at Pylos, Mycenae and Thebes, confirming the script's use across the wider Mycenaean world.

summary: After c. 1450 BC the Knossos archives are kept in Linear B — an adaptation of Minoan Linear A used to write Greek.
significance: The clearest evidence that Mycenaean Greeks had taken control of Knossos and Minoan Crete.
body:
After around 1450 BC, the palace administration at Knossos on Crete began keeping its records in Linear B, an early form of Greek, instead of the Minoan Linear A.

The tablets record flocks, textile production, chariot components, land, workers, and offerings to gods including Poseidon and a "Mistress of the Labyrinth". They are administrative records covering roughly a single cycle, not literature or a royal chronicle. Unfired clay was a temporary medium; the archive survived only because destruction fire accidentally baked it hard.

That the language is Greek is decisive: Greek-speakers were administering Crete from Knossos after the destruction of most other Cretan palace centres. Linear B was adapted from Linear A and fits Greek awkwardly, omitting final consonants and collapsing several sounds into the same signs. Its decipherment pushed the attested history of Greek back some five centuries beyond Homer while exposing the economic routines behind palace power.

The Knossos archive was not an isolated case. Comparable Linear B archives, using the same script and administrative conventions to record the same kind of Greek, were later excavated at Pylos, Mycenae and Thebes on the mainland, confirming that this bureaucratic writing system was a shared feature of Mycenaean palace administration generally, rather than a peculiarity of the Cretan centre alone.

name: The Trojan War (traditional)

claims.text: Greek tradition dated the Trojan War to the late 13th or early 12th century BC.
Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BC.
Hittite texts record a place Wilusa and a power called Ahhiyawa.
A Mycenaean Greek conflict at Troy occurred in some form.
The Iliad preserves an accurate account of a historical campaign.
Helen, Achilles and Agamemnon were historical individuals.

summary: The ten-year siege of Troy by a Greek coalition under Agamemnon — the central event of Greek legend, and possibly of Greek memory.
significance: The central event of Greek legend, the setting of the Iliad and the Odyssey, and the point from which Greeks counted their past.
body:
The war in which, according to Greek legend, an alliance of Greek kings besieged Troy, in north-western Asia Minor, for ten years. Ancient scholars dated it variously; the date calculated by Eratosthenes, with Troy falling in 1184 BC, became the standard one, and Greeks counted their heroic past from it.

In the legend, the Trojan prince Paris carried off Helen, wife of King Menelaus of Sparta, after the goddess Aphrodite promised her to him as a reward for judging her the most beautiful of three goddesses. Menelaus' brother Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, led a great fleet against Troy. After ten years of siege, in which heroes such as Achilles and Hector died, the Greeks took the city by hiding warriors inside a wooden horse. The war and its aftermath are the subject of the *Iliad*, the *Odyssey* and a cycle of lost epics, and of much later Greek tragedy.

Greeks treated the war as history, though not uncritically: Herodotus reasoned that if the Trojans had truly been holding Helen, they would have given her back. Modern evidence fits a real conflict of some kind. Troy VIIa, a level of the site at Hisarlik, was destroyed by fire around 1180 BC, with arrowheads and unburied bodies in the ruins. Hittite archives name a city called Wilusa in this region, troubled by a power called Ahhiyawa — most likely the Mycenaean Greeks.

What the evidence does not support is the war as Homer tells it: a thousand ships, a single ten-year siege, a coalition of named kings. The poems took shape some four centuries later and blend memory with the world of their own time. Most scholars now hold that something happened at Troy involving mainland Greeks, and that the *Iliad* is inspired by its memory rather than a record of it.

name: Destruction of the Mycenaean palaces

claims.text: All major Mycenaean palace centres were destroyed or abandoned c. 1200–1180 BC.
Linear B literacy ceased with the palace system.
Late defensive works indicate the palaces anticipated a threat.
A single cause explains the destructions.
A Dorian invasion caused the collapse.
The collapse coincided with wider disruption across the eastern Mediterranean, including the fall of the Hittite empire and Egyptian records of the "Sea Peoples".

summary: Every major Mycenaean palace was destroyed or abandoned within a generation, ending palatial civilisation in Greece.
significance: The collapse of Mycenaean civilisation, which ended writing, palaces and centralised states in Greece for centuries.
body:
Between about 1200 and 1180 BC the palaces of Mycenaean Greece were destroyed or abandoned.

Pylos burned in a single catastrophic fire that baked its archive hard. Mycenae and Tiryns were damaged and their citadels subsequently contracted to a fraction of their former extent. Thebes was destroyed outright. Within perhaps thirty years the entire interconnected palace system across the Greek mainland was gone, and with it Linear B literacy, large-scale monumental construction, fresco painting, and the centralised administrative apparatus that had organised agricultural production and craft manufacture for centuries.

The collapse was not an isolated Greek event: it coincided closely with wider upheaval across the entire eastern Mediterranean and Near East, including the fall of the powerful Hittite empire in Anatolia and Egyptian temple inscriptions describing repeated invasions by loosely defined groups modern historians call the "Sea Peoples," whose composition and origins remain genuinely uncertain. No single cause for the Aegean collapse specifically is agreed among specialists. Candidate explanations include a prolonged drought documented in pollen cores from the period, a cluster of destructive earthquakes, internal revolt against the palace elites, disruption of the long-distance tin trade needed for bronze production, and straightforward raiding or invasion. The late investment several palaces made in stronger fortifications and secured underground water supplies suggests their rulers saw some specific threat coming, even if they could not stop it.

Some smaller settlements continued at a reduced scale after the destructions, and pottery styles evolve gradually rather than vanishing overnight, which argues this was a systems failure — the collapse of a specific, centralised way of organising society — rather than a sudden, total depopulation of the Greek mainland. But whatever the precise mixture of causes, nobody built anything resembling a palace in Greece again for roughly six hundred years.

name: The Sea Peoples

claims.text: Egyptian inscriptions name multiple groups attacking in coalition c. 1177 BC.
Reliefs depict them moving with families and possessions.
"Sea Peoples" is a modern term, not an ancient collective name.
They were a symptom of the collapse as much as a cause.
They constituted a single unified nation or invasion.
Some named groups, including the Peleset, are widely thought to be connected to the later Philistines of the Levantine coast.

summary: Coalitions of displaced peoples attacked Egypt and the Levant by land and sea during the Bronze Age Collapse.
significance: The attacks most closely linked with the collapse of the Late Bronze Age world around 1200 BC.
body:
Between about 1200 and 1150 BC, coalitions of peoples from the Aegean and Anatolia attacked Egypt and the coasts of the eastern Mediterranean, at the time when the great states of the Late Bronze Age were collapsing.

Egyptian inscriptions of the pharaohs Merneptah (around 1208 BC) and Ramesses III (around 1177 BC) name the attackers: Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh, Sherden and others, fighting together. Ramesses III's reliefs at Medinet Habu show them defeated on land and at sea, and show families travelling in ox-carts, which suggests a migration rather than a raid. His inscription says these peoples had already destroyed the Hittite Empire, Carchemish, Arzawa and Alashiya (Cyprus) — places where archaeologists do find destruction layers at this time.

The name "Sea Peoples" is modern; no ancient text uses it as a single label. Historians now see them less as the cause of the Bronze Age collapse than as part of it: populations uprooted by drought, famine, earthquakes and the failure of states, who then spread the disruption further.

Some of the groups can be traced afterwards. The Peleset are generally identified with the Philistines, who settled on the southern coast of Canaan, bringing Aegean-style pottery, and whose name survives in "Palestine". The Sherden and Shekelesh may be linked with Sardinia and Sicily.

name: Fall of Hattusa

claims.text: Hattusa was destroyed by fire and abandoned around 1190 BC.
Archives and valuables appear to have been removed before the destruction.
Late Hittite texts record grain shortages and emergency imports.
The fall of Hattusa left the eastern Mediterranean without any single dominant great power for generations, reshaping the regional balance for centuries.

summary: The Hittite capital was burned and abandoned around 1190 BC, ending one of the great powers of the Late Bronze Age.
significance: The fall of the Hittite Empire, one of the great powers of the Late Bronze Age and a key event of the Bronze Age collapse.
body:
Hattusa in central Anatolia had been the seat of an empire that fought Egypt to a draw at Kadesh. Around 1190 BC it burned and was abandoned.

Excavation suggests the collapse was not simply violent: the royal archives and treasuries appear to have been emptied before the fire, and parts of the city were already being abandoned. This looks like a state coming apart, then a final destruction.

The Hittite archives include letters recording grain shortages and appeals for emergency shipments in the empire's last decades — direct testimony to the food crisis behind the wider collapse.

The consequences outlasted the empire itself by centuries: with Hatti gone, Egypt weakened, and the palace states of the Aegean destroyed in the same rough window, the eastern Mediterranean and Near East entered a long period without any single power capable of the kind of diplomatic and military reach the Hittites, Egyptians and Mycenaeans had each once exercised, a genuine power vacuum that later states like Assyria and, eventually, the Greek poleis themselves would only gradually come to fill.

name: Destruction of Ugarit

claims.text: Ugarit was destroyed around 1185 BC and never reoccupied.
Final letters record enemy ships and absent defensive forces.
Ugaritic scribes used an early cuneiform alphabetic script.
Ugarit's destruction is one of a wave of roughly contemporary city destructions across the eastern Mediterranean around 1200-1150 BC.

summary: The Syrian port of Ugarit was destroyed around 1185 BC, its final letters still in the kiln.
significance: A vivid case study of the Bronze Age collapse, documented in the city's own last letters.
body:
Ugarit, a wealthy port on the coast of northern Syria, was destroyed around 1185 BC.

Ugarit was a wealthy cosmopolitan port whose archives are written in at least eight languages, and whose scribes developed a cuneiform alphabet of thirty signs.

The last letters found there are extraordinary. The king writes that enemy ships have appeared, that his own fleet is away in Lycia and his troops in Hatti, and that the country is undefended. Another asks the king of Alashiya for help. Some were found still in the kiln where they were being baked, never sent.

The city was destroyed and never reoccupied. The tablets were preserved by the fire that ended it.

Ugarit did not fall in isolation. Its destruction sits within a broader wave of city burnings and abandonments across the eastern Mediterranean world clustered within a few decades either side of 1200 BC, from Hattusa in Anatolia to sites across the Levant and the Aegean, a synchronised pattern of collapse that is the central evidence historians use to define the Bronze Age Collapse as a connected regional crisis rather than a series of unrelated local disasters.

name: The Ionian migration

claims.text: Greek settlement expanded along the western Anatolian coast from c. 1050 BC.
Dialect distribution in Anatolia matches the traditional migration pattern.
Ionia became the leading centre of early Greek intellectual activity.
The migration was organised and led from Athens as tradition claims.
The twelve cities of Ionia later formed a religious and political league centred on the Panionion sanctuary.

summary: Greek-speaking populations settled the western coast of Anatolia, founding the cities of Ionia.
significance: The movement that created Ionia, the Greek coast of Asia Minor where Greek philosophy and science would begin.
body:
Between about 1050 and 900 BC, after the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, Greek-speaking settlers established themselves on the central west coast of Asia Minor and its islands.

Greek tradition held that refugees from the mainland, led from Athens, settled the Anatolian coast after the collapse. Archaeology confirms Greek material culture appearing at Miletus, Ephesus, Colophon and elsewhere from around 1050 BC — though at Miletus there had already been Mycenaean presence.

The dialect map supports the tradition: Ionic in the centre, Aeolic to the north, Doric to the south, matching the claimed origins of the settlers.

Ionia became the most economically and intellectually dynamic part of the Greek world. Homer, Thales, Anaximander, Heraclitus, Hecataeus and Herodotus all came from this coast.

The twelve principal Ionian cities eventually formalised their shared identity by forming a loose religious and political league, meeting periodically at a common sanctuary called the Panionion on the slopes of Mount Mycale, a rare instance of Greek cities from different, often rival poleis maintaining a durable collective institution built specifically around their claimed common ancestry.

name: The Lefkandi hero burial

claims.text: The Lefkandi Toumba building dates to c. 1000–950 BC.
It covered a double burial with four sacrificed horses.
Grave goods included Near Eastern and Cypriot imports.
The find substantially revised the "Dark Age" model.
The building's colonnaded design is seen by many archaeologists as an early ancestor of later Greek peripteral temple architecture.

summary: A monumental building erected over a rich double burial with four sacrificed horses, around 1000 BC.
significance: The find that overturned the idea of an empty, impoverished Dark Age in Greece.
body:
Around 1000–950 BC at Lefkandi, on the island of Euboea, a man and a woman were buried with great wealth beneath a monumental building.

The Toumba building at Lefkandi was 50 m long with an external colonnade — three centuries before any comparable Greek structure — and was deliberately demolished and buried under a mound soon after construction.

Beneath it: a cremated man in a Cypriot bronze amphora with an iron sword; an inhumed woman with gold hair-coils, a gold pectoral and a Babylonian pendant already 700 years old when buried; and a shaft with four horses.

The find dismantled the assumption that the Dark Age was uniformly poor and disconnected. Elite wealth, monumental building, heroic burial ritual and long-distance imports were all present at the supposed low point.

The building's form itself is architecturally suggestive: its external row of posts running around an apsidal structure anticipates, in rough outline, the peripteral colonnade that would become the defining feature of the Greek temple centuries later, leading many archaeologists to see the Toumba building as an early, isolated ancestor of a design principle that would not become standard again for a very long time.

name: Adoption of the Greek alphabet

claims.text: The Greek alphabet derives from a Phoenician consonantal script.
Greeks repurposed unused Phoenician consonant signs as vowel letters.
The earliest Greek alphabetic inscriptions date to c. 750–740 BC.
The earliest known inscriptions are informal rather than administrative.
The alphabet was adopted specifically to record Homeric epic.
The transmission route most likely ran through Greek traders and mercenaries in contact with Phoenician communities such as at Al Mina in Syria.

summary: Greeks adapted the Phoenician consonantal script and repurposed unused signs as vowels — creating the first full alphabet.
significance: The creation of the first full alphabet, with vowels — the ancestor of the Latin and Cyrillic scripts and the basis of Greek literature.
body:
Some time in the early 8th century BC, probably through trading contacts in the eastern Mediterranean, Greeks adopted the Phoenician script and turned it into the first full alphabet. Linear B, the earlier Mycenaean script, had been forgotten for four centuries.

Phoenician writing recorded only consonants, which suited Semitic languages built on consonant roots. Greek needs vowels to be read clearly. The Greeks took Phoenician signs for consonants that Greek did not have — *aleph*, *he*, *yod*, *ayin* — and used them for vowels: alpha, epsilon, iota, omicron. They also added new letters. The result could write any Greek word unambiguously and could be learned quickly, unlike the scripts of the palace scribes.

The most likely place of transfer was a mixed trading settlement where Greeks and Phoenicians lived side by side, such as Al Mina in Syria, or Crete, Rhodes or Cyprus. Local variants of the alphabet soon developed in different Greek regions; the Euboean version passed to the Etruscans and then to the Romans, becoming the Latin alphabet.

The earliest Greek inscriptions, from around 740–720 BC, are not accounts. The Dipylon Oinochoe from Athens offers a jug as a prize for the best dancer, and Nestor's Cup from Pithekoussai carries a joking verse about drinking. From the start, the alphabet recorded poetry and everyday life — and soon the Homeric epics themselves.

name: The first Olympiad

claims.text: Greek chronology was reckoned in four-year Olympiads from a traditional start of 776 BC.
Votive dedications at Olympia increase markedly in the 8th century BC.
The Games continued for more than a millennium.
Games were actually first held in 776 BC.
An Olympic truce was proclaimed before each festival, in principle allowing athletes and spectators safe passage across warring Greek states.

summary: The traditional date of the first Olympic Games, which became the anchor of Greek chronology.
significance: The fixed point from which Greeks counted time, and the symbolic start of the Archaic period.
body:
By tradition the first Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Elis in 776 BC.

Greek historians dated events by counting four-year Olympiads from 776 BC, the year the runner Koroibos of Elis was said to have won the *stadion*. It gave the Greek world its first shared chronological framework — essential for a civilisation of hundreds of independent states with their own calendars and magistrate-year dating.

Archaeology at Olympia shows dedications increasing sharply in the eighth century, consistent with a festival growing in importance around then, though it cannot confirm a specific year.

The Games ran for over a thousand years until Theodosius I suppressed pagan festivals around AD 393.

Before each celebration, heralds travelled the Greek world announcing a sacred truce, the *ekecheiria*, which in theory suspended hostilities and guaranteed safe passage for athletes, spectators and religious envoys travelling to and from Olympia — a rare mechanism for imposing a temporary peace across a world of perpetually warring city-states, even though the truce was sometimes violated in practice.

name: Greek colonisation of the Mediterranean

claims.text: Greeks founded settlements across the Mediterranean and Black Sea c. 750–550 BC.
Colonies were politically independent of their mother cities.
Delphi was routinely consulted before colonial foundations.
The Latin alphabet descends from Greek script transmitted via Etruria.
Land shortage was the principal driver of colonisation.
Cumae in Italy, founded by Euboean settlers, is generally reckoned the earliest permanent Greek colony in the west.
Naucratis in Egypt functioned as a controlled trading enclave rather than a fully independent colony.

secondaryImage.caption: The Greek temples of Paestum (Poseidonia), founded by colonists from Sybaris in southern Italy.

summary: Between roughly 750 and 550 BC Greeks founded hundreds of settlements from Spain to the Black Sea.
significance: The movement that spread Greek cities and culture from Spain to the Black Sea and created the wider Greek world.
body:
Between about 750 and 550 BC Greek cities founded hundreds of new settlements around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, from Spain to the Crimea. The main causes were shortage of land at home, political conflict that pushed losing factions abroad, and trade.

A colony (*apoikia*, "settlement away from home") was sent out by a mother city under a founder (*oikistes*), who was often honoured as a hero after his death. Founders usually consulted the oracle at Delphi first. The new city was independent from the start, keeping religious and sentimental ties to its mother city but not obeying it.

The Euboean cities of Chalcis and Eretria led the way, trading at Al Mina in Syria and settling Pithekoussai and then Cumae in Italy by the mid-8th century BC. Corinth founded Syracuse and Corcyra; Achaean cities founded Sybaris and Croton in southern Italy, which became known as Magna Graecia ("Great Greece"); Miletus founded dozens of settlements around the Black Sea, from Sinope to Olbia; Megara founded Byzantion; Thera founded Cyrene in Libya; and Phocaea founded Massalia (Marseille) in Gaul. In Egypt, Greeks traded at Naukratis under the pharaoh's control rather than founding an independent city.

The results shaped the whole ancient world. Greek cities came to ring the Mediterranean and Black Sea "like frogs around a pond", as Plato put it. The Greek alphabet passed to the Etruscans and from them to the Romans, and Greek wine, olive oil, pottery, coinage and religion spread among the peoples the colonists met.

name: The invention of coinage

claims.text: The earliest standardised stamped coinage was produced in Lydia in the late 7th century BC.
The first coins were struck in electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy.
Croesus introduced separate gold and silver coinages.
Athenian silver coinage circulated widely beyond Athenian territory.
The earliest coins were struck on only one face, with the reverse showing only the punch mark used to strike them.

summary: Lydia produced the first standardised stamped coins in electrum in the late seventh century BC; Greek cities adopted the idea within a generation.
significance: The invention of coined money, which the Greek cities quickly made their own.
body:
In the late 7th century BC, in the kingdom of Lydia in western Asia Minor, the first true coins were struck.

They were small lumps of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver washed down the Pactolus river near the capital, Sardis. Each was of a fixed weight and stamped with a design, at first on one face only, the back carrying the rough mark of the punch. The stamp guaranteed the coin, so it could be counted rather than weighed and tested at every exchange — the step that turned metal into money. The best-known early type shows a lion's head, the badge of the Lydian kings. Some of the earliest well-dated examples were found in a foundation deposit of the temple of Artemis at Ephesus.

Because electrum's gold content varies, King Croesus (c. 560–546 BC) introduced separate coins of refined gold and silver, the first two-metal system.

The Greek cities of Ionia copied the idea at once, and within a century it had spread across the Greek world. Coins became a badge of each city's identity: the turtle of Aegina, the colt of Corinth, the owl of Athens. Athens' silver owls, minted from the mines of Laurion, were trusted from Egypt to the Black Sea.

Today coin hoards are among archaeologists' most precise dating tools.

name: The reforms of Solon

claims.text: Solon cancelled debts and prohibited loans secured on the person.
He created four property-based classes determining eligibility for office.
He extended jury participation and the right to prosecute on another's behalf.
He redistributed land.
Solon also revised Athenian weights, measures and currency standards as part of his broader economic reforms.

summary: Solon cancelled debts, abolished debt-slavery and opened office by wealth rather than birth, defusing a crisis at Athens.
significance: The reforms that ended debt slavery in Athens and broke the link between birth and political power.
body:
Athens in 594 BC faced revolt: farmers were falling into debt-bondage and being sold abroad. Solon was given extraordinary powers to legislate.

The *seisachtheia* cancelled existing debts, freed those enslaved for them, and outlawed loans secured on the person. He then replaced birth with income as the qualification for office, creating four property classes, and gave even the poorest citizens the right to sit on juries and to prosecute on behalf of a wronged party — the first general right of legal action.

He left Athens for a decade so he could not be pressured to change the laws. He satisfied nobody fully, and said so in his own poetry.

Alongside these political and legal changes, Solon is also credited with adjusting Athens's weights, measures and coinage standards, encouraging craft specialisation and trade by, among other things, granting citizenship to foreign artisans willing to settle permanently in Athens — measures aimed at broadening the city's economic base beyond the indebted small farmers whose crisis had triggered his appointment in the first place.

name: The Peisistratid tyranny

claims.text: Peisistratus and his sons controlled Athens from 561 to 510 BC with interruptions.
Hipparchus was assassinated in 514 BC by Harmodius and Aristogeiton.
Hippias was expelled from Athens in 510 BC with Spartan assistance.
The tyrannicides acted for political rather than personal motives.
Athenians later commissioned a bronze statue group of the Tyrannicides, one of the first known public monuments honouring named individuals rather than gods.

summary: Peisistratus and his sons ruled Athens for half a century, expanding festivals and public works before being expelled.
significance: A tyranny that strengthened Athens' institutions, festivals and public works, preparing the ground for democracy.
body:
Peisistratus and his sons ruled Athens, with interruptions, from 561 to 510 BC.

Peisistratus took power three times, ruling securely from 546 BC. His regime was not straightforwardly repressive: he kept Solon's laws, sent judges into the countryside to reduce dependence on local aristocrats, funded public works and water supply, expanded the Panathenaia, and gave the City Dionysia its dramatic competitions.

His sons Hippias and Hipparchus succeeded him. Hipparchus was assassinated in 514 BC by Harmodius and Aristogeiton — over a personal quarrel, though Athens later remembered them as democratic martyrs and put up the first political statues in Greek history. Hippias grew harsh and was expelled in 510 BC with Spartan help. He later guided the Persians to Marathon.

The bronze group of the Tyrannicides that Athens erected in their honour was itself a landmark: it is generally considered among the earliest public monuments in the Greek world to celebrate specific, named human individuals rather than gods or mythical figures, a striking honour for two men whose actual motive, by most contemporary accounts, was a personal grudge rather than any conscious plan to restore civic freedom.

name: The reforms of Cleisthenes

claims.text: Cleisthenes created ten tribes composed of trittyes from three separate regions.
The Council of 500 was selected by lot, fifty from each tribe.
Citizens were registered through their deme.
The reforms were designed to break regional aristocratic power.
The reforms followed directly on the expulsion of the tyrant Hippias and a brief factional struggle between Cleisthenes and the rival aristocrat Isagoras.

summary: Athens was reorganised into ten artificial tribes drawn from across Attica, creating the structure of democracy.
significance: The founding of Athenian democracy: the institutions that gave political power to the whole citizen body.
body:
In 508/7 BC the Athenian aristocrat Cleisthenes reorganised the city's citizen body and institutions.

The reforms followed almost immediately on the expulsion of the tyrant Hippias and a short, sharp factional struggle between Cleisthenes and a rival aristocrat, Isagoras, who briefly gained the upper hand with Spartan military backing before Cleisthenes, having appealed directly to the ordinary Athenian populace for support, prevailed and pushed his new constitution through.

Cleisthenes divided Attica into three regions — city, coast, inland — split each into ten *trittyes*, and built each new tribe from exactly one trittys drawn from each of the three regions. A tribe therefore had no real geographical coherence and no single aristocratic patron capable of dominating it, which deliberately destroyed the regional power bases that had driven roughly a century of destabilising factional conflict among Athens's leading families.

Citizenship was registered by *deme*, the local ward or village, and a citizen's demotic — his deme name — replaced his father's name (his patronymic) in official public contexts, substituting residence for inherited lineage as the basic mark of civic identity. The new Council of 500, with fifty members chosen by lot from each of the ten tribes, prepared the agenda for the full citizen assembly, and its presiding committee of fifty rotated through ten separate terms across the year, so that at any given moment a different tenth of the Council held day-to-day administrative responsibility.

The overall result was a system in which most ordinary male citizens could reasonably expect to hold some public office at least once in their lifetime, and in which the underlying machinery of government itself was deliberately built to resist capture or long-term domination by any single family or faction.

name: The Ionian Revolt

claims.text: Ionian Greek cities revolted against Persian rule from 499 to 493 BC.
Athens and Eretria sent naval support to the rebels.
Sardis was burned during the revolt.
Persia destroyed Miletus in 494 BC.
Aristagoras's failed expedition against Naxos, undertaken with Persian backing, is generally seen as the immediate trigger for the revolt.

summary: The Greek cities of Asia Minor rebelled against Persian rule; Athens sent help, and Persia did not forget it.
significance: The rebellion that drew Athens into conflict with Persia and led directly to the Persian invasions of Greece.
body:
A rebellion by the Greek cities of Ionia, on the west coast of Asia Minor, against Persian rule, lasting from 499 to 493 BC. Our main account is Herodotus.

It began with a failure. Aristagoras, the tyrant of Miletus, had led a Persian-backed attack on the island of Naxos that collapsed. Facing the consequences, he turned to revolt, giving up his own tyranny and urging the other Ionian cities to expel theirs. Herodotus says Aristagoras' father-in-law Histiaeus, held at the Persian court, sent him the signal to rebel tattooed on the shaved head of a slave.

Sparta refused to help, but Athens sent twenty ships and Eretria five. In 498 BC the rebels marched inland and burned Sardis, the seat of the Persian governor, though they soon withdrew. The revolt spread to the Hellespont, Caria and Cyprus. Persia then reconquered the region city by city. In 494 BC the Ionian fleet was defeated at Lade off Miletus, after the Samian ships deserted, and Miletus was taken, its men killed and its women and children deported. In Athens, the playwright Phrynichus' *Capture of Miletus* so upset its audience that he was fined.

The revolt's real importance was what followed. Athens' small part in it, and the burning of Sardis, gave Darius I a reason to punish Athens and Eretria. Herodotus says he had a servant remind him at every meal to "remember the Athenians". The punitive expedition of 490 BC ended at Marathon, and so began the Persian Wars.

name: Battle of Marathon
outcome: Decisive Greek victory

claims.text: Athenian and Plataean forces defeated a Persian army at Marathon in 490 BC.
The Greek centre was deliberately thinned to extend the line.
The Athenian dead were buried in a mound on the battlefield.
Herodotus' casualty figures are accurate.
The Persian expedition was commanded by Datis and Artaphernes and guided by the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias.
The modern marathon footrace is inspired by, but not directly attested in, the ancient tradition of a runner carrying news of the victory to Athens.

summary: Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeated a larger Persian landing force in 490 BC — the first Greek victory over Persia.
significance: The first Greek victory over a Persian army on land: it kept Athens independent, and became the founding memory of Athenian democracy.
body:
Fought in 490 BC on the coastal plain of Marathon, about 40 km north-east of Athens. A Persian expedition under Datis and Artaphernes, sent by Darius I to punish Athens and Eretria for supporting the Ionian Revolt, had already sacked Eretria. It landed at Marathon with the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias, whom it meant to restore to power.

About 10,000 Athenian hoplites and 1,000 Plataeans — the only allies to come — faced a larger Persian force, now usually estimated at around 25,000. At the urging of the general Miltiades the Greeks attacked, advancing at a run across the last stretch of open ground to limit their exposure to Persian archers. Their centre was deliberately thinned and their wings strengthened; the wings broke the Persians opposite and turned inward on the centre. Herodotus gives 6,400 Persian dead against 192 Athenians, who were buried in the mound (the Soros) that still stands on the plain.

The Athenians then marched back to the city in time to deter the Persian fleet, which had sailed round Cape Sounion. The story of a runner dying after announcing the victory is a later legend; Herodotus' runner, Pheidippides, ran to Sparta before the battle to ask for help. The legend inspired the marathon race at the first modern Olympics in 1896.

Marathon did not end the Persian threat, which returned on a far larger scale under Xerxes ten years later. But it showed that a hoplite phalanx could beat Persian infantry in the open, and Athenians remembered it ever after as their finest hour.

name: Battle of Thermopylae
outcome: Persian victory; Greek rearguard annihilated

claims.text: A Greek force held the pass at Thermopylae for three days in 480 BC.
The position was turned by a mountain path revealed to the Persians.
Persian arrowheads excavated on Kolonos hill confirm the final stand.
Around 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans remained at the end.
Xerxes' army numbered in the millions.
Leonidas reportedly replied "Come and take them" (molon labe) when Xerxes demanded the Greeks surrender their weapons.
A memorial epigram by Simonides, commemorating the Spartan dead, was inscribed at the site.

summary: A Greek force under Leonidas held the pass for three days against Xerxes' army before being outflanked and destroyed.
significance: The most famous last stand in history: a defeat that became a lasting symbol of resistance against overwhelming odds.
body:
Fought over three days in August 480 BC at the pass of Thermopylae in central Greece, between a Greek force under King Leonidas of Sparta and the invading army of the Persian king Xerxes. At the same time the Greek fleet fought the Persian navy off Artemisium nearby.

About 7,000 Greeks held the pass where it narrowed to a few metres between the mountains and the sea, behind an old Phocian wall. There Persian numbers counted for little, and for two days every assault failed, including attacks by the royal guard, the Immortals. Later tradition gives Leonidas famous replies — "come and take them" when told to surrender his arms — that may be invented.

A local man, Ephialtes, then showed the Persians a mountain path that led behind the Greek position. Learning they were about to be surrounded, Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with his 300 Spartans, about 700 Thespians, who chose to remain, and around 400 Thebans. On the third day they were surrounded and killed on a small hill, shot down by archers. In 1939 Spyridon Marinatos found many Persian arrowheads there.

Thermopylae was a defeat, and the Persians went on to burn Athens. But the stand delayed Xerxes, let the fleet withdraw safely, and became the most famous example of courage against overwhelming odds. The poet Simonides wrote the epitaph for the Spartan dead: "Stranger, tell the Spartans that here we lie, obedient to their words."

name: Battle of Salamis
outcome: Decisive Greek naval victory

claims.text: The Greek fleet defeated a larger Persian fleet at Salamis in 480 BC.
The battle was fought in narrow straits that negated Persian numbers.
Themistocles used deception to bring on the engagement.
Aeschylus was present at the battle.
The Athenian population had been evacuated to Salamis, Aegina and Troezen before the battle under a decree associated with Themistocles.
Xerxes reportedly watched the battle from a throne set up on a hillside overlooking the strait.

summary: The Greek fleet destroyed a much larger Persian navy in the narrows off Salamis, breaking the invasion.
significance: The naval victory that broke Xerxes' invasion and saved Greek independence.
body:
Fought in September 480 BC in the straits between the island of Salamis and the coast of Attica, between the Greek allied fleet and the navy of Xerxes.

With Athens itself evacuated under a decree traditionally credited to Themistocles — its population moved to the nearby island of Salamis, to Aegina, and to Troezen on the Peloponnesian mainland — and now burning behind them, the Greek fleet of around 370 ships faced a Persian fleet Herodotus numbers in the many hundreds, though modern estimates are considerably more conservative than his figures. The allied commanders, worried by the exposed position, wanted to withdraw south to the Isthmus of Corinth and make their stand there instead; Themistocles argued forcefully for fighting in the narrow straits at Salamis instead, and reportedly forced the issue by secretly sending his own servant, Sicinnus, to Xerxes with a message claiming the Greeks were divided and about to flee under cover of darkness — luring the Persian king into blocking both exits from the strait overnight rather than letting the Greek fleet slip away intact.

Xerxes, having taken the bait, is said to have had a throne set up on a hillside overlooking the strait so that he could watch his fleet destroy the Greeks at his leisure. In the narrows, however, the Persian fleet's numerical advantage became a liability: ships fouled and collided with one another in the cramped space, and the heavier, sturdier Greek triremes rammed methodically into the resulting confusion, breaking the Persian battle line apart.

Aeschylus, who fought in the battle himself, staged it eight years later in his tragedy *The Persians*, telling the story from the perspective of the grieving Persian court back in Susa rather than from the Greek side — the only surviving Greek tragedy to dramatise a contemporary historical event rather than myth, and remarkable for having been written by a participant in the very battle it depicts.

name: Battle of Plataea
outcome: Decisive Greek victory; Persian land forces destroyed

claims.text: A Greek coalition destroyed the Persian land army at Plataea in 479 BC.
Mardonius was killed in the battle.
It was among the largest hoplite engagements recorded.
The Greek victory at Mycale occurred at nearly the same time.
Pausanias, the Spartan regent who commanded the Greek forces, was later disgraced amid accusations of Medism and treasonous dealings with Persia.
Spoils from the battle funded the Serpent Column dedicated at Delphi, listing the participating Greek states.

summary: The largest hoplite battle ever fought ended the Persian invasion of Greece in 479 BC.
significance: The battle that ended the Persian invasion of Greece for good.
body:
Fought in August 479 BC near Plataea in southern Boeotia, between the Greek allies under the Spartan regent Pausanias and the Persian army of Mardonius, which had stayed in Greece after Xerxes went home following Salamis.

About 40,000 Greek hoplites, with many lighter troops — the largest Greek army yet assembled — faced the Persians across the Asopus river. For days the two sides manoeuvred over water and supplies, while Persian cavalry harassed the Greeks. A confused Greek withdrawal by night left the allied army scattered, and Mardonius, thinking it was retreating, attacked.

The Spartans and the Tegeans beside them held firm under Persian arrows and then charged. In close fighting the lightly armoured Persian infantry could not stand against the hoplites. Mardonius was killed, and the Persian army broke and fled; its fortified camp was stormed. On the same day, tradition says, the Greek fleet destroyed the Persian navy's base at Mycale in Asia Minor.

The victory ended the Persian invasion of Greece. From the spoils, the Greeks dedicated at Delphi the Serpent Column, a bronze pillar inscribed with the names of the 31 allied states; its base survives in Istanbul, where Constantine moved it. Pausanias himself later fell under suspicion of treason with Persia and was starved to death in a temple in Sparta. The initiative passed to the Greeks, and soon after to Athens and its Delian League.

name: The Delian League

claims.text: The Delian League was founded in 478/7 BC with its treasury on Delos.
The treasury was moved to Athens in 454 BC.
Athenian Tribute Lists record annual payments by member states.
Athens used force to prevent members from leaving.
League funds were used for the Acropolis building programme.
The treasury's move to Athens in 454 BC was officially justified by the threat of Persian naval power after an Athenian disaster in Egypt.
The League dissolved after Athens's defeat in the Peloponnesian War in 404 BC.

summary: An alliance against Persia founded in 478 BC that Athens converted within a generation into an empire.
significance: The alliance that won the Aegean back from Persia and became the Athenian empire whose tribute paid for the Parthenon.
body:
An alliance of Greek states, mostly islands and coastal cities of the Aegean, formed under Athenian leadership in 478 BC, after the Persian invasion of Greece had been defeated. Its purpose was to continue the war against Persia and free the Greek cities still under Persian rule. It lasted until Athens' defeat in 404 BC.

Members swore to have the same friends and enemies, and contributed either ships or money to a common treasury kept on the sacred island of Delos, where the League's council met. Under the Athenian general Cimon it drove Persian forces out of the Aegean, winning a great victory at the Eurymedon around 466 BC.

As the Persian threat faded, the League became an Athenian empire. Members that tried to leave — Naxos around 470 BC, Thasos in 465 BC — were besieged and forced back. Most allies chose to pay money rather than supply ships, so only Athens kept a fleet. In 454 BC the treasury was moved from Delos to Athens, and tribute soon paid for Pericles' buildings on the Acropolis. Athens imposed its coinage and measures on its allies, settled cleruchies (colonies of Athenian citizens) on their land, and moved important court cases to Athens.

The Athenian Tribute Lists, inscriptions recording the share of each ally's payment given to Athena, survive on stone and show who paid what year by year. Resentment of Athenian rule was one of the causes of the Peloponnesian War, in which Sparta claimed to be fighting to free the Greeks. With Athens' surrender in 404 BC the League was dissolved.

name: Construction of the Parthenon

claims.text: The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BC.
Its horizontal lines curve and its columns incline inward.
A Venetian bombardment detonated an Ottoman powder store inside in 1687.
Roughly half the surviving sculpture was removed by Lord Elgin.
The architectural refinements were intended as optical corrections.
The Parthenon replaced an earlier, unfinished temple on the site destroyed by the Persians in 480 BC.
The building has served in later centuries as a Christian church and, under Ottoman rule, as a mosque.

secondaryImage.caption: Sculptures from the Parthenon removed by Lord Elgin, now in the British Museum.

summary: The temple of Athena Parthenos was built on the Acropolis in fifteen years, funded substantially by imperial tribute.
significance: The building of the greatest temple of Classical Greece, and the defining monument of Athens at the height of its power.
body:
The Parthenon, the temple of Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis of Athens, was built between 447 and 432 BC, as the centrepiece of Pericles' building programme. Its architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates, and the sculptor Pheidias directed its sculpture and its great gold-and-ivory statue of Athena. It was paid for largely from the tribute of Athens' allies in the Delian League.

It replaced an earlier, unfinished marble temple destroyed when the Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 BC; drums from its columns were built into the Acropolis wall as a reminder. Around 22,000 tonnes of marble were brought from Mount Pentelicus, 16 km away. The temple is a Doric building of 8 by 17 columns, with Ionic features such as the continuous frieze around its inner building. Its sculptures included the frieze of a procession, 92 metopes showing mythical battles, and pediments showing the birth of Athena and her contest with Poseidon for Athens.

Almost nothing in it is straight. The platform curves up about 11 cm in the middle, the columns lean slightly inwards and swell gently along their height (*entasis*), and the corner columns are thicker. These refinements, cut into every block in advance, are usually explained as corrections for optical illusions, though no ancient source confirms it.

The building later became a church and then, under Ottoman rule, a mosque. In 1687, during a Venetian siege, a shell ignited gunpowder stored inside and blew out its centre. Between 1801 and 1812 agents of Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving sculpture, now in the British Museum; Greece has long sought its return.

name: The Peloponnesian War
outcome: Spartan victory; Athenian empire dissolved

claims.text: Athens and Sparta fought from 431 to 404 BC, ending in Athenian defeat.
Plague struck Athens in 430 BC, killing a large proportion of the population.
Persian subsidies funded the Spartan fleet in the final phase.
Athens surrendered after the loss of its fleet at Aegospotami.
Thucydides' analysis of the war's cause is broadly correct.

In the Melian Dialogue, Thucydides has Athenian envoys tell the neutral island of Melos that "the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must" before Athens besieged it, executed its men and enslaved its women and children.
The uneasy Peace of Nicias of 421 BC collapsed within a few years, and fighting resumed well before the Sicilian Expedition.

summary: Twenty-seven years of war between Athens and Sparta that exhausted Greece and ended the Athenian empire.
significance: The war that ended Athens' empire and its Golden Age, and exhausted the Greek city-states.
body:
The war fought from 431 to 404 BC between Athens and its Delian League empire on one side and Sparta and its Peloponnesian League allies on the other. Thucydides, who fought in it and wrote its history, saw the real cause in the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

The first phase, the Archidamian War (431–421 BC), set a land power against a sea power. Pericles brought the people of Attica inside the city walls and relied on the fleet and the Long Walls to the port of Piraeus, while Spartan armies ravaged the countryside. The overcrowded city was struck by plague in 430 BC, which killed perhaps a quarter of its people, Pericles among them. Athenian success at Sphacteria in 425 BC and Spartan success under Brasidas in the north led to the Peace of Nicias in 421 BC.

The peace never really held. Sparta won a major land battle at Mantinea in 418 BC, and in 416 BC Athens conquered the neutral island of Melos, killing its men and enslaving its women and children. Then in 415–413 BC Athens sent a huge expedition against Syracuse in Sicily, which ended with its entire army and fleet destroyed.

In the final phase (413–404 BC) Sparta fortified a base in Attica and, with Persian money, built a fleet. Athens fought on and won at Arginusae in 406 BC, but in 405 BC the Spartan admiral Lysander destroyed its last fleet at Aegospotami, cutting off its grain supply from the Black Sea. Athens surrendered in 404 BC; its empire was dissolved and its Long Walls pulled down, and the oligarchy of the Thirty briefly took power.

Both sides came out exhausted. The real winner was Persia, which by the King's Peace of 387 BC regained control of the Greek cities of Asia Minor.

name: The Plague of Athens

claims.text: An epidemic struck Athens from 430 BC and recurred through 426 BC.
Thucydides contracted the disease and recorded its symptoms in detail.
Pericles died of the disease in 429 BC.
A mass burial of the period has been excavated in the Kerameikos.
The disease was typhoid fever.
Overcrowding caused by the wartime evacuation of the Attic countryside behind Athens's Long Walls is generally seen as having worsened the epidemic's spread.

summary: An epidemic in the overcrowded wartime city killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including Pericles.
significance: A catastrophe that killed Pericles and perhaps a quarter of Athens' people, and changed the course of the Peloponnesian War.
body:
An epidemic struck Athens in 430 BC, the second year of the Peloponnesian War, and returned in 429 and 427–426 BC.

The epidemic struck a city already swollen well beyond its normal population, since Pericles's wartime strategy had deliberately brought the entire rural population of Attica inside Athens's fortified Long Walls to shelter from Spartan invasion, packing refugees into makeshift housing and temporary shelters with none of the sanitation a smaller, ordinary population could rely on — conditions modern historians generally agree made the disease's spread dramatically worse than it might otherwise have been.

Thucydides himself caught the disease, survived it, and described its progress with unusually clinical detachment: fever, inflamed eyes, bleeding from the mouth and throat, pustules covering the body, unquenchable thirst, and death typically arriving on the seventh or eighth day for those who did not recover. He explains that he wrote the description in such careful detail specifically so that the disease could be recognised again if it ever returned — an explicitly scientific motive, unusual for the period, that treats his own eyewitness suffering as useful data rather than simply personal testimony.

He also recorded the disease's corrosive social effects in unflinching detail: people died entirely untended because those who tried to nurse them caught the illness themselves and died alongside them, corpses were left piled in temples for lack of anywhere else to put them, ordinary funeral rites broke down completely, and open lawlessness spread as people, believing they might die at any moment regardless of behaviour, saw no remaining reason to restrain themselves for a future they no longer expected to have.

Proposed modern identifications of the actual disease include typhus, typhoid fever, smallpox, measles and a viral haemorrhagic fever similar to Ebola. A DNA study of dental pulp from a mass grave excavated in the Kerameikos cemetery in 2006 suggested typhoid fever specifically, but the analysis has been contested by other researchers on grounds of possible contamination, and the true identity of the disease remains formally unresolved.

name: The Sicilian Expedition

claims.text: Athens launched an expedition against Syracuse in 415 BC that was destroyed by 413 BC.
Alcibiades promoted the expedition and defected after being recalled.
The Athenian fleet was destroyed in the Great Harbour of Syracuse.
Surviving prisoners were held in the stone quarries.
Plutarch reports that some captured Athenians won better treatment from their captors by reciting verses of Euripides, whose poetry Syracusans especially admired.

summary: Athens sent its largest ever expedition against Syracuse; it was annihilated, and the empire never recovered.
significance: The disaster that turned the Peloponnesian War against Athens.
body:
The Athenian expedition against Syracuse in Sicily in 415–413 BC, during a lull in the Peloponnesian War. Athens hoped to conquer the richest Greek city of the west and add Sicily's wealth and grain to its empire.

Alcibiades urged the attack; the cautious general Nicias opposed it and, trying to deter the Assembly, said a huge force would be needed. The Assembly voted him exactly that: about 130 warships and over 5,000 hoplites, under Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus. Soon after the fleet sailed, Alcibiades was recalled to face charges of sacrilege, and instead fled to Sparta, where he advised the Spartans against Athens.

The Athenians besieged Syracuse but moved slowly. Lamachus was killed, and the Spartan general Gylippus arrived to organise the defence and break the Athenian siege wall. Large reinforcements under Demosthenes in 413 BC failed to turn the tide. The Athenian fleet was defeated in the Great Harbour of Syracuse, and an attempt to break out by land ended in disaster. Nicias and Demosthenes were executed; thousands of prisoners were held in the stone quarries of Syracuse, where many died. Plutarch says some won better treatment by reciting Euripides.

Athens lost perhaps 40,000 men in all, including allies, and some 200 ships. Thucydides called it the greatest event of the war. Persia and Athens' subject allies saw their chance, Sparta built a fleet, and although Athens fought on for nine more years, the Sicilian disaster turned the war decisively against it.

name: Battle of Aegospotami
outcome: Decisive Spartan victory

claims.text: Lysander captured the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BC.
The Athenian ships were taken while beached and largely unmanned.
The defeat cut Athens off from Black Sea grain and forced surrender.
Alcibiades warned the Athenian commanders beforehand.
The Athenian commander Conon escaped with a handful of ships and fled to Cyprus rather than surrender.

summary: Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet on the beach in 405 BC, ending the Peloponnesian War within months.
significance: The defeat that lost Athens the Peloponnesian War: with its last fleet gone, the city was starved into surrender within months.
body:
Fought in 405 BC at Aegospotami ("Goat Rivers") on the European shore of the Hellespont, between the Spartan fleet under Lysander and the last fleet of Athens.

The Athenian fleet was beached on an open shore in the Hellespont with no proper base, and its crews dispersed daily to find food. Lysander watched this for four days. On the fifth he attacked while the ships were empty and captured almost the entire fleet — around 170 ships — with barely a fight.

Alcibiades, living nearby in exile, had ridden down to warn the Athenian commanders that their position was indefensible. They told him to go away.

With the fleet gone, the Black Sea grain route was cut. Athens was starved out and surrendered in 404 BC.

Not every Athenian ship was taken. The commander Conon, seeing the disaster unfold, broke out with eight or nine triremes and sailed for Cyprus rather than surrender or return to face an Athens he knew would blame its generals; he would later resurface years afterward leading a Persian-funded fleet that helped restore Athenian naval power after the war.

name: The trial of Socrates

claims.text: Socrates was tried in 399 BC on charges of impiety and corrupting the young.
He was convicted and executed by hemlock.
He declined an opportunity to escape.
The prosecution was politically motivated.
Plato's Apology reports the actual defence speech.
Xenophon's separate account of the trial largely corroborates Plato's on the major points, despite differences in emphasis and detail.

summary: Socrates was tried before 500 Athenian jurors for impiety and corrupting the young, convicted, and executed.
significance: The trial in which democratic Athens condemned its most famous philosopher, and the founding moment of Western philosophy's account of itself.
body:
In 399 BC the philosopher Socrates was tried in Athens before a jury of 500 citizens.

The charges were introducing new gods and corrupting the youth. The political background is unavoidable: Athens had lost the war, suffered the Thirty Tyrants, and several of Socrates' associates — Critias, Charmides, Alcibiades — had been prominent in the oligarchy or its betrayals. An amnesty barred prosecuting them for it, but not this.

Plato's *Apology* has Socrates refuse to plead for mercy, compare himself to a gadfly stinging a sluggish horse, and propose free meals at public expense as his counter-penalty. He was convicted by around 280 to 220; more jurors voted for death than for conviction, suggesting the counter-proposal cost him.

He declined an arranged escape, arguing that having accepted the city's laws all his life he could not repudiate them when they went against him, and drank hemlock.

Plato was not the only student to leave an account. Xenophon, who was not present at the trial, wrote his own version based on what participants told him, and while the two accounts differ in tone and selective detail — Xenophon's Socrates is notably more concerned with practical matters like avoiding the infirmities of old age — they agree on the essential shape of events: the charges, the roughly even vote, and Socrates' calm, unyielding defiance of the jury.

name: Battle of Leuctra
outcome: Decisive Theban victory

claims.text: Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC.
Epaminondas massed his left wing to unusual depth against the Spartan right.
Around 400 of 700 Spartiates present were killed.
Spartan power declined irreversibly after the battle.
Epaminondas's oblique deep-column tactic at Leuctra directly influenced Philip II's own later development of the Macedonian phalanx.

summary: Epaminondas destroyed the myth of Spartan invincibility with a massed left wing, killing 400 of 700 Spartiates present.
significance: The battle that ended Spartan supremacy in Greece and showed how tactics could beat a reputation.
body:
Fought in July 371 BC at Leuctra in southern Boeotia, between Thebes and its Boeotian allies under Epaminondas and a Spartan army under King Cleombrotus. Sparta was trying to break up the Boeotian League that Thebes led.

Greek armies normally put their best troops on the right wing, so the strongest units of two armies rarely met. Epaminondas reversed this. He massed his left wing fifty ranks deep, directly against the Spartan king and his best troops on the Spartan right, and held his weaker right wing back. The Theban cavalry drove off the Spartan horse, and the deep Theban column, led by the elite Sacred Band, smashed the Spartan right before the rest of the lines had properly engaged.

Cleombrotus was killed, along with about 400 of the 700 full Spartan citizens (Spartiates) present. With perhaps only 1,500 Spartiates left in all, this was a loss Sparta could not replace. The myth of Spartan invincibility, which had lasted for centuries, was broken in an afternoon.

Thebes followed up immediately. In 370–369 BC Epaminondas invaded Laconia, the first enemy army to do so in living memory, and freed Messenia, whose helots had farmed the land on which the Spartan system depended. Thebes became the leading power in Greece until Epaminondas' death at Mantinea in 362 BC. The young Philip II of Macedon, then a hostage in Thebes, learned from his methods.

name: Accession of Philip II

claims.text: Philip II took power in Macedon in 359 BC after the death of Perdiccas III.
He restructured the Macedonian army around the sarissa phalanx.
Control of the Pangaeum mines gave Macedon substantial annual revenue.
Philip also secured his early reign through a network of strategic marriages to daughters of neighbouring ruling families.

summary: Philip took control of a Macedon that had just lost its king and 4,000 men, and began the reforms that would make it dominant.
significance: The beginning of Macedon's rise from a weak kingdom to the master of Greece.
body:
In 359 BC Philip II became ruler of Macedon, at first perhaps as regent for his infant nephew, after his brother King Perdiccas III was killed in battle.

Perdiccas III was killed by the Illyrians with 4,000 Macedonians. Macedon faced simultaneous threats from Illyrians, Paeonians, Thracians and two rival claimants backed by Athens. Philip initially acted as guardian for the young Amyntas IV before taking the kingship himself, a transition whose precise constitutional form is obscured by later sources.

Philip bought off some enemies, defeated others, and rebuilt the army around the sarissa, deeper infantry formations and coordinated cavalry. He took Amphipolis and the Pangaeum gold mines, which gave him roughly 1,000 talents a year — more than Athens' entire imperial revenue at its height.

Within five years the immediate threats were gone. Within twenty-one, he controlled Greece.

Diplomacy did as much as the battlefield to stabilise his early reign: Philip married a rapid succession of women from neighbouring royal and noble houses, including Olympias of Epirus, each match binding a potentially hostile or useful neighbouring power more closely to Macedon, a strategy of marriage-as-alliance he pursued throughout his reign alongside his military reforms.

name: Battle of Chaeronea
outcome: Decisive Macedonian victory

claims.text: Philip II defeated an allied Greek army at Chaeronea in 338 BC.
The Theban Sacred Band was destroyed in the battle.
A mass grave of 254 men lies beneath the Lion of Chaeronea.
Alexander commanded the cavalry on the Macedonian left.
Demosthenes, who had campaigned for years to unite Athens and its allies against Philip, fought in the battle and later admitted to fleeing the field.
The Lion of Chaeronea monument marks the mass grave believed to hold the Theban Sacred Band.

summary: Philip II defeated the Athenian-Theban alliance in 338 BC, ending the independence of the Greek city-states.
significance: The battle that ended the independence of the Greek city-states and made Macedon master of Greece.
body:
Fought in August 338 BC at Chaeronea in western Boeotia, between Philip II of Macedon and an alliance of Greek states led by Athens and Thebes, brought together by the Athenian orator Demosthenes.

Each side had around 30,000 men. Philip commanded the Macedonian right; his eighteen-year-old son Alexander led the Companion Cavalry on the left, facing the Thebans. Philip's wing made a controlled withdrawal, drawing the Athenians forward. As they pressed on, the allied line stretched and a gap opened between the Athenians and the Thebans. Alexander charged into it, Philip turned and attacked, and the Greek army collapsed.

The Theban Sacred Band held its ground and was destroyed almost to a man. A mass grave of 254 men found beneath the Lion of Chaeronea, the monument raised over the Theban dead, is almost certainly theirs. Demosthenes, fighting in the ranks, fled with the rest; about a thousand Athenians were killed and two thousand captured.

Philip treated Athens leniently, valuing its fleet and prestige, but dealt harshly with Thebes, placing a garrison in its citadel. In 337 BC he united the Greek states in the League of Corinth under his leadership and announced a war against Persia. Chaeronea ended the independence of the Greek city-states. Philip's murder in 336 BC left the war with Persia to Alexander.

name: The League of Corinth

claims.text: The League of Corinth was established in 337 BC with Philip II as hegemon.
Sparta refused to join.
The League authorised a joint campaign against Persia.
Macedonian garrisons were stationed at key Greek cities.
The Athenian orator Isocrates had argued for years, before the League's founding, that a Panhellenic war against Persia was the only cure for Greek infighting.

summary: Philip organised the Greek states into a federal league under his leadership, with a mandate to invade Persia.
significance: The union that gave Macedon formal leadership of Greece and a mandate for Alexander's invasion of Persia.
body:
In 337 BC, after his victory at Chaeronea, Philip II of Macedon called the Greek states to Corinth and organised them into a league.
