Formed in 337 BC, the League guaranteed members' constitutions, banned constitutional change by force, prohibited internal warfare, and elected Philip *hegemon* of a joint campaign against Persia. Sparta alone refused to join, and was left alone.

The legal form was a voluntary alliance of free states. The practical reality included Macedonian garrisons at Corinth, Thebes and Chalcis, and a ban on precisely the political changes that might threaten Macedonian influence.

It was the framework under which Alexander invaded Asia, and it gave the campaign the character of Panhellenic revenge for 480 BC rather than simple conquest. The idea itself was not new: the aging Athenian orator Isocrates had spent years publicly arguing that only a united Greek war against Persia could redirect the constant internal warfare between Greek cities into something more productive, and he addressed an open letter to Philip urging exactly this role on him shortly before the League was actually formed.

name: Assassination of Philip II

claims.text: Philip II was assassinated at Aegae in 336 BC by his bodyguard Pausanias.
Pausanias was killed immediately while fleeing.
Ancient sources attribute a personal grievance as the motive.
Olympias or Alexander was involved in the plot.
Persia sponsored the assassination.
Philip was assassinated on the very eve of the Panhellenic invasion of Persia he had spent years organising, a campaign Alexander would inherit and carry out instead.

summary: Philip was murdered at his daughter's wedding in 336 BC by his bodyguard Pausanias, on the eve of the Persian invasion.
significance: The murder that put the 20-year-old Alexander on the throne of Macedon on the eve of the invasion of Persia.
body:
Philip II of Macedon was assassinated in 336 BC in the theatre at Aigai, the old Macedonian capital, during his daughter's wedding celebrations.

The wedding at Aegae was a spectacle: Philip walked into the theatre without guards, deliberately, between statues of the twelve gods and a thirteenth of himself. Pausanias of Orestis, one of his own bodyguards, stabbed him and ran for horses waiting outside. He tripped and was killed on the spot.

The ancient explanation is personal: Pausanias had been assaulted by associates of Attalus and Philip had failed to give him justice. That the assassin was killed immediately, and that horses were waiting, has always invited suspicion of a wider plot.

Suspects proposed in antiquity and since include Olympias, sidelined by Philip's newest marriage; Alexander, whose succession was threatened by a potential heir of pure Macedonian blood; and Persia. There is no decisive evidence for any of them.

Whoever was responsible, the timing was extraordinary: Philip had spent his final years assembling the League of Corinth and an advance force already sent ahead into Asia Minor for the great Panhellenic invasion of Persia he had long planned to lead personally, and his murder handed that fully prepared campaign, army and justification directly to his twenty-year-old son instead.

name: Battle of the Granicus
outcome: Macedonian victory

claims.text: Alexander defeated a Persian satrapal army at the Granicus in 334 BC.
His life was saved during the cavalry fighting by Cleitus.
Greek mercenaries in Persian service were massacred or enslaved after the battle.
He dedicated captured armour at Athens with an inscription excluding Sparta.
The victory secured Alexander's control of the Asia Minor coastline and opened the way for the Greek cities there to be "liberated" from Persian rule.

summary: Alexander's first victory in Asia, won by charging across a river against the Persian satrapal army.
significance: Alexander's first victory in Asia, which opened Asia Minor to his conquest.
body:
Fought in May 334 BC at the Granicus river in north-western Asia Minor, between Alexander and the armies of the local Persian governors.

The Persian satraps drew up on the far bank of the Granicus with cavalry along the top and Greek mercenary infantry behind. Parmenion advised waiting for dawn. Alexander attacked immediately, leading the Companions across the river at an angle.

The fighting around him was desperate — a Persian axe split his helmet, and Cleitus the Black cut off the arm of the man about to finish him. Alexander would later kill Cleitus in a drunken quarrel.

After the cavalry broke, the Greek mercenaries were surrounded and massacred; the survivors were sent to forced labour in Macedon as traitors to the Panhellenic cause. Alexander sent 300 captured Persian panoplies to Athens, dedicated to Athena, with an inscription pointedly noting they came from "Alexander and the Greeks, except the Spartans".

Beyond the immediate fighting, Granicus had a decisive strategic effect: it broke organised Persian resistance along the Asia Minor coast, allowing Alexander to move rapidly from city to city presenting himself as liberator of the Greek cities there from Persian-backed rule, a propaganda framing that did real diplomatic work in easing his advance even where local populations were, in practice, simply exchanging one distant master for another.

name: Battle of Issus
outcome: Decisive Macedonian victory

claims.text: Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus in 333 BC.
The narrow terrain prevented the Persians from using their numerical advantage.
Darius' family was captured and treated with respect.
Darius offered substantial territorial concessions afterwards.
The battle is depicted in the Alexander Mosaic, a Roman floor mosaic likely copying a lost Hellenistic painting.

summary: Alexander defeated Darius III in person on a narrow coastal plain, capturing the Persian royal family.
significance: Alexander's first defeat of Darius in person, which opened the Levant and Egypt to his conquest.
body:
Fought in November 333 BC on the narrow coastal plain at Issus, near modern Iskenderun in south-eastern Turkey, between Alexander the Great and the Persian king Darius III, the first time the two kings met in battle.

Darius made a clever move, marching his army round behind Alexander and cutting his supply line. But in doing so he brought his much larger army onto a narrow strip of land between the mountains and the sea, where it could not use its numbers.

Alexander led the Companion Cavalry across the Pinarus river in a charge aimed straight at Darius himself. Further along the line the Macedonian phalanx struggled to cross the riverbed against Darius' Greek mercenaries and suffered heavy losses. But when Darius turned and fled, the Persian army lost heart and collapsed.

The Persian camp was captured with Darius' mother, wife and daughters. Alexander kept their royal rank and treated them with marked respect. Darius later offered a great ransom, all lands west of the Euphrates and a daughter in marriage. Plutarch says Parmenion remarked that he would accept if he were Alexander, and Alexander replied that so would he, if he were Parmenion.

The victory opened the coast of Syria and Phoenicia, and then Egypt, to Alexander. The battle is shown in the famous Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii.

name: Siege of Tyre

claims.text: Alexander besieged Tyre for approximately seven months in 332 BC.
He constructed a causeway from the mainland to the island city.
The causeway permanently connected the island to the shore.
The population was massacred or enslaved after the city fell.
Alexander crucified a number of surviving Tyrian men along the shore as a further reprisal after the city's capture.

summary: Alexander took the island city of Tyre after seven months by building a causeway to it from the mainland.
significance: Alexander's greatest siege, which removed the last Persian naval base in the eastern Mediterranean.
body:
Alexander besieged Tyre, the leading Phoenician city on the coast of modern Lebanon, for seven months in 332 BC.

Tyre stood on an island 800 m offshore behind walls rising from the sea, and refused Alexander entry. He could not leave a Persian naval base behind him, so he built a mole out to the island — quarrying the abandoned mainland city for stone.

The Tyrians burned his siege towers with a fireship, dropped rocks to foul the approaches, and dropped heated sand on attackers, which got inside armour. Alexander eventually assembled a fleet from Sidon and Cyprus, blockaded both harbours, and mounted siege engines on lashed ships.

When the wall was breached the city was sacked: sources report 8,000 killed and 30,000 sold into slavery. The mole silted up and permanently joined Tyre to the mainland — a geographic change still visible on any map.

Beyond the killing and enslavement, ancient sources add a further, deliberately public punishment: several thousand surviving Tyrian men of military age were reportedly crucified along the coastline in view of the sea, a severity that other Phoenician and Levantine cities weighing whether to resist Alexander's advance could hardly fail to take note of.

name: Founding of Alexandria

claims.text: Alexander founded Alexandria in Egypt in 331 BC.
The site provided a double harbour and access to inland waterways.
Alexander visited the oracle of Ammon at Siwa.
He was greeted at Siwa as the son of the god.
Alexander himself never saw the city develop, since he left Egypt shortly after founding it and died before returning.

summary: Alexander laid out a new city on the Egyptian coast that became the intellectual capital of the ancient world.
significance: The foundation of the city that became the capital of Ptolemaic Egypt and the intellectual centre of the Greek world.
body:
Alexander founded Alexandria in 331 BC on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, at the western edge of the Nile Delta.

Alexander chose a site on a limestone ridge between the sea and Lake Mareotis, with the island of Pharos providing a natural double harbour and freshwater access inland. It was an outstanding choice of site, and the city has been continuously important for 2,300 years.

The story goes that, lacking chalk, the surveyors marked the street plan with barley meal, and birds descended and ate it — read by the seers as a sign that the city would feed the world.

Alexander also travelled to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa, deep in the desert, and was reportedly greeted as son of the god. What he asked and was told, he never disclosed.

Alexander left Egypt soon after laying out the city's plan and never returned; he died in Babylon eight years later without ever seeing Alexandria built up into the city it would become. That work fell instead to his successor Ptolemy I, who made it the capital of his new kingdom and set in motion the building projects, library and museum that turned Alexander's coastal outline into the greatest city of the Hellenistic world.

name: Battle of Gaugamela
outcome: Decisive Macedonian victory; Persian empire collapses

claims.text: Alexander defeated Darius III at Gaugamela on 1 October 331 BC.
A Babylonian astronomical record fixes the date precisely.
Darius had the battlefield levelled in advance for chariots.
Alexander broke off pursuit to relieve Parmenion on the left.
Darius fielded fifteen war elephants at Gaugamela, among the first Persian forces used in battle against Macedon.
Babylon and Susa surrendered to Alexander without resistance in the aftermath of the battle.

summary: Alexander destroyed the main Persian army on 1 October 331 BC, effectively ending the Achaemenid Empire.
significance: The decisive battle of Alexander's war with Persia: after it, the Achaemenid Empire was his.
body:
Fought on 1 October 331 BC at Gaugamela, on the plain east of the Tigris near modern Mosul, between Alexander the Great and Darius III.

Darius, having learned some hard lessons from Issus, chose a wide open plain this time and had it deliberately levelled so his scythed chariots and superior cavalry numbers could actually be brought to bear, and assembled contingents drawn from across the length of the empire, including Bactrians, Scythians and, for the first time in a battle against Macedon, fifteen war elephants — an animal Alexander's army had never yet faced in combat and one whose psychological effect on unfamiliar troops and horses could matter as much as its practical battlefield use.

Alexander advanced obliquely toward the Persian right, deliberately drawing the Persian line further and further sideways to avoid being outflanked himself. When that stretching finally opened a gap in the Persian centre-left, he wheeled the Companion cavalry into a wedge and drove it directly at Darius's own position, exploiting the same weakness that had already broken the Persian king's nerve once before at Issus.

Darius fled the field again rather than risk capture. On the Macedonian left, meanwhile, the general Parmenion was nearly overwhelmed by Persian and allied cavalry, and Persian forces reached and looted part of the Macedonian baggage camp; Alexander was forced to break off his pursuit of the fleeing Darius to ride back and relieve Parmenion's hard-pressed wing. The Persian empire's central field army, though, was effectively finished as a fighting force — Babylon and Susa, two of its greatest cities, surrendered to the advancing Macedonians without any resistance at all in the weeks that followed.

A Babylonian astronomical diary, an independent cuneiform record kept for entirely unrelated purposes, notes a lunar eclipse occurring eleven days before the battle, giving modern historians an unusually precise, externally verified date for Gaugamela: 1 October 331 BC.

name: The burning of Persepolis

claims.text: The palace complex at Persepolis was destroyed by fire in 330 BC.
Alexander captured an enormous treasury at Persepolis.
The fire preserved administrative tablets by baking them.
The burning was deliberate policy rather than a drunken act.
Persepolis was never rebuilt as a functioning capital afterward, though the site retained ceremonial and symbolic importance.

summary: Alexander burned the Achaemenid ceremonial capital in 330 BC — whether as policy or on a drunken impulse is disputed.
significance: The symbolic end of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and a lasting puzzle about Alexander's aims.
body:
Alexander burned the palaces of Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Persian kings in south-western Iran, in spring 330 BC.

Alexander took Persepolis in early 330 BC and its treasury, reportedly 120,000 talents, more than any state in the Greek world had ever held.

Months later the palace complex burned. Arrian, following Ptolemy, presents it as a deliberate act of vengeance for Xerxes' burning of Athens, and records Parmenion arguing against destroying what was now Alexander's own property. Diodorus, Curtius and Plutarch describe a drunken feast at which the Athenian courtesan Thais urged that a woman's hand should avenge the Acropolis, and Alexander threw the first torch.

Excavation confirms an intense fire — burnt cedar beams, ash layers, melted metal. It cannot say why. The fire also baked the administrative tablets in the fortification walls, preserving them.

Whatever the motive, the destruction was effectively final: Persepolis was never restored as a working royal residence afterward, even though the site continued to carry symbolic weight for Persian identity for centuries, later becoming a point of reference for Sasanian kings keen to associate themselves with Achaemenid grandeur even as the palace itself lay in ruins.

name: Battle of the Hydaspes
outcome: Macedonian victory; Porus reinstated as satrap

claims.text: Alexander defeated Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BC.
Porus deployed a large force of war elephants.
Alexander crossed the river upstream under cover of a storm.
Bucephalus died at or shortly after the battle.
It was the costliest battle of Alexander's career.
Porus was reinstated and expanded as a Macedonian client ruler after the battle, on Alexander's own initiative.

summary: Alexander's hardest-fought victory, against Porus and his war elephants in monsoon rain on the Jhelum river.
significance: Alexander's hardest battle and his last great victory, fought at the eastern limit of his conquests.
body:
Fought in May 326 BC on the Hydaspes (modern Jhelum) river in the Punjab, between Alexander the Great and Porus, an Indian king who ruled the land beyond the river. It was Alexander's last great battle.

The river was swollen by monsoon rains, and Porus held the far bank with perhaps 200 war elephants, which horses will not face. Alexander spent weeks staging noisy movements along the bank at night until Porus' scouts stopped responding. Then he crossed for real some 27 km upstream, hidden by a violent storm.

The battle was among the hardest of his career. Alexander's cavalry drew off and defeated the Indian horse. The phalanx opened lanes to let the charging elephants through, then attacked their drivers and their trunks; maddened, wounded elephants trampled soldiers on both sides. Eventually the Indian army was surrounded and broke.

Porus fought on bravely until captured. Asked how he wished to be treated, he is said to have replied "like a king". Alexander restored him to his kingdom and enlarged it. Alexander's horse Bucephalus died around this time, and Alexander founded the city of Bucephala in its memory, along with another, Nicaea.

Soon afterwards, at the Hyphasis river, Alexander's exhausted army refused to go further east, and he turned back.

name: Death of Alexander

claims.text: Alexander died at Babylon in June 323 BC after an illness of about eleven days.
Babylonian astronomical diaries independently record the death.
He left no adult heir capable of holding the empire together.
He was poisoned.
The "to the strongest" succession remark was actually made.
His body was later hijacked en route to Macedon by Ptolemy, who diverted it to Egypt for burial.

summary: Alexander died at Babylon in June 323 BC aged 32, leaving no viable heir and an empire that fragmented immediately.
significance: The end of Alexander's reign and the beginning of the Hellenistic age, as his generals fought over his empire.
body:
Alexander the Great died at Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BC, aged 32.

He fell ill after a prolonged banquet and declined over eleven days with fever, becoming unable to speak. Soldiers filed past his bed; he could only move his eyes. He died on 10 or 11 June 323 BC.

His wife Roxana was pregnant; his half-brother Arrhidaeus had a cognitive disability. Asked who should succeed, he reportedly said "to the strongest" — which is what happened, over forty years of wars among his generals. Both his son and his half-brother were eventually murdered.

Causes proposed include malaria, typhoid, acute pancreatitis, West Nile virus, complications from the untreated lung wound he took in India, and poison. Plutarch, writing four centuries later, notes that no suspicion of poison arose at the time. The Babylonian astronomical diaries record the king's death independently, confirming the date.

Even his corpse became a political prize. The funeral cortège, elaborately built to carry the body back to Macedon for burial, was intercepted in Syria by Ptolemy, who diverted it to Egypt — first to Memphis and later to Alexandria — a calculated move that helped legitimise his own claim to be Alexander's true successor.

name: Wars of the Diadochi
outcome: Empire divided into Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms

claims.text: Alexander's generals fought for control of the empire from 322 to 281 BC.
The successors assumed royal titles from 306 BC.
Alexander's surviving family members were killed during the conflicts.
The wars produced three principal successor kingdoms.
Antigonus the One-Eyed, the general who came closest to reuniting Alexander's whole empire, was killed at the battle of Ipsus in 301 BC in his eighties, still fighting on foot after his cavalry fled.

summary: Forty years of war among Alexander's generals that carved the empire into the Hellenistic kingdoms.
significance: The wars that divided Alexander's empire into the kingdoms of the Hellenistic world.
body:
The wars fought between about 322 and 281 BC by the Diadochi ("successors") — Alexander the Great's generals — over his empire after his death at Babylon in 323 BC.

At first the generals claimed to govern for Alexander's heirs: his half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus, who was mentally unfit to rule, and his infant son Alexander IV. Perdiccas, the first regent, was murdered in 320 BC, and the empire was divided among governors who soon fought each other. One by one Alexander's family were killed: Philip III, his mother Olympias, Alexander IV and his mother Roxana, and Alexander's sister Cleopatra. From 306 BC, starting with Antigonus and his son Demetrius, the generals took the title of king.

Antigonus the One-Eyed came closest to reuniting the empire, but the other kings allied against him, and he was killed at Ipsus in Phrygia in 301 BC, one of the largest battles of the age, decided by Seleucus' war elephants. The last of Alexander's original generals fought at Corupedium in 281 BC, where Seleucus killed Lysimachus, only to be murdered himself months later.

By then the shape of the Hellenistic world was fixed: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Syria, Mesopotamia and Iran, and the Antigonid descendants of Demetrius in Macedon, with smaller kingdoms such as Pergamon and Bactria emerging later. These kingdoms lasted until Rome absorbed them in the 2nd and 1st centuries BC. Our main narrative source is Diodorus, who followed the lost history of Hieronymus of Cardia.

name: Battle of Ipsus
outcome: Antigonus killed; unified empire permanently ended

claims.text: Antigonus I was defeated and killed at Ipsus in 301 BC.
Seleucus deployed around 400 war elephants obtained from India.
The elephants prevented Demetrius' cavalry from rejoining the battle.
The battle ended prospects of reuniting Alexander's empire.
The victors divided Antigonus's territory among themselves, a partition that set the basic map of the Hellenistic kingdoms for the following century.

summary: The largest battle of the Diadochi wars, where Seleucus' 400 elephants decided the fate of Alexander's empire.
significance: The battle that ended any chance of reuniting Alexander's empire and fixed the shape of the Hellenistic kingdoms.
body:
Fought in 301 BC at Ipsus in Phrygia, central Asia Minor, between Antigonus I and his son Demetrius on one side and the allied kings Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander on the other.

Antigonus the One-Eyed came closest to reuniting Alexander's empire, which is why the others allied against him. At Ipsus in Phrygia perhaps 150,000 men met.

Demetrius drove off the opposing cavalry and pursued too far. Seleucus then interposed his 400 war elephants — obtained from Chandragupta Maurya in exchange for eastern territory — as a screen between Demetrius and the battlefield. Horses will not approach elephants, and Demetrius could not get back.

Antigonus, aged around 80, was left unsupported and killed by javelins, reportedly still expecting his son to return. With him died the last realistic prospect of a single empire.

The victors carved up his territory among themselves rather than reuniting it under one ruler: Lysimachus took most of Anatolia, Seleucus gained Syria, and Cassander and Ptolemy consolidated their existing holdings. This partition, more than any single treaty, fixed the basic territorial pattern of Macedon, the Seleucid empire, Egypt and the smaller Anatolian kingdoms that would define the Hellenistic world for the next hundred years.

name: Battle of Salamis (Cyprus)
outcome: Decisive Antigonid naval victory; triggered royal titles across the Successor states

claims.text: Demetrius Poliorcetes defeated a Ptolemaic fleet off Salamis in 306 BC and took control of Cyprus.
Ptolemy's relief fleet numbered roughly 140 ships.
News of the victory led Antigonus I and Demetrius to proclaim themselves kings, and the other Successors followed within about a year.
The battle is treated as marking the start of open, independent Hellenistic kingship.
Demetrius went on to besiege Rhodes the following year, an operation so costly it gave rise to the phrase "siege of Rhodes" as a byword for a huge, ultimately failed undertaking.

summary: Demetrius Poliorcetes destroyed a Ptolemaic fleet off Cyprus — a victory that pushed the Successors to start calling themselves kings.
significance: A naval victory that led Antigonus and Demetrius to take the title of king — and the other Successors to follow, formally ending the fiction of Alexander's united empire.
body:
Fought in 306 BC off Salamis on the east coast of Cyprus, between Demetrius Poliorcetes, son of Antigonus I, and the fleet of Ptolemy I of Egypt.

Demetrius invaded Cyprus, then held by Ptolemy, defeated Ptolemy's brother Menelaus and besieged him in the city of Salamis. Ptolemy sailed to the rescue with about 140 warships. Demetrius met him in open water outside the harbour and won an overwhelming victory: most of Ptolemy's fleet was sunk or captured, along with thousands of soldiers. Ptolemy escaped to Egypt, and Menelaus surrendered the city and the whole island.

The battle had a political consequence far beyond Cyprus. On hearing the news, Antigonus had himself and Demetrius proclaimed kings (*basileus*) — the first of Alexander's successors to take the title openly. All of Alexander's own family had by then been killed. Within about a year Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander had all done the same. The pretence that they were governing a single empire for Alexander's heirs was over; from now on there were rival Hellenistic kingdoms.

The next year Demetrius turned on Rhodes, Ptolemy's ally, with a vast siege that failed. Ptolemy recovered Cyprus in 295 BC, and it remained a Ptolemaic possession until the Roman period.

name: Founding of the Library of Alexandria

claims.text: The Ptolemies founded a Museum and Library at Alexandria in the early 3rd century BC.
Resident scholars were salaried and housed by the state.
Alexandrian scholars produced critical editions of Homer and invented textual sigla.
Callimachus produced a catalogue of the collection.
The Library was destroyed in a single catastrophic event.
Eratosthenes, one of the Library's directors, used its resources to calculate the circumference of the Earth with striking accuracy.

summary: The Ptolemies founded a Museum and Library that salaried scholars and attempted to collect every book in the world.
significance: The creation of the ancient world's greatest centre of scholarship and science.
body:
Around 295–283 BC Ptolemy I, and then his son Ptolemy II, founded the Museum and Library in the royal quarter of Alexandria, the new capital of Ptolemaic Egypt. The adviser behind the project was probably Demetrius of Phalerum, a former ruler of Athens and student of Aristotle's school.

The Museum — a "shrine of the Muses" — was a research institution. Its scholars received salaries, free lodging and meals, and exemption from taxes, and were free to pursue their work. The Library set out to collect every Greek book. Ships in the harbour reportedly had their books seized and copied, with the owners getting the copies; Ptolemy III is said to have borrowed Athens' official texts of the great tragedians against a huge deposit, and kept the originals. The collection's size is unknown; ancient figures range up to 700,000 scrolls.

Its scholars created the tools of textual scholarship. Zenodotus, Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus produced critical editions of Homer, marking doubtful lines with signs still used by editors. The poet Callimachus compiled the *Pinakes*, a catalogue of Greek literature in 120 books. The librarian Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference, and Alexandria became the centre of Greek mathematics, astronomy and medicine.

The Library did not disappear in one great fire. A fire during Julius Caesar's war in Alexandria in 48 BC destroyed some books; royal support faded; and Ptolemy VIII drove out many scholars in 145 BC. It declined over centuries, and when it finally ceased to exist is unknown.

name: Eratosthenes measures the Earth

claims.text: Eratosthenes estimated the Earth's circumference from shadow angles at two locations.
Greek astronomers already accepted that the Earth is spherical.
His result was accurate to within a few percent of the true value.
The method assumed Syene lay exactly on the Tropic of Cancer and due south of Alexandria, simplifications that were not perfectly accurate but did not fatally undermine the result.

summary: Using shadow angles at two Egyptian cities, Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference to within a few percent.
significance: One of the great achievements of ancient science: the first reasoned measurement of the size of the Earth.
body:
Around 240 BC Eratosthenes of Cyrene, head of the Library of Alexandria, calculated the circumference of the Earth.

The method requires only a stick, a well and a measured distance. At Syene the sun was directly overhead at noon on the summer solstice — no shadow in a deep well. At Alexandria, roughly due north, a vertical gnomon cast a shadow of about 7.2° at the same moment.

If the Earth is a sphere and the sun's rays are effectively parallel, that 7.2° is 1/50th of a full circle, so the distance between the cities is 1/50th of the circumference. Multiplying by 50 gave about 250,000 stades.

How accurate this is depends on the length of his stade, which is not certain. On the most probable value the error is under 2%. That the Earth is spherical was already standard among educated Greeks — Aristotle had argued it from the shape of the shadow during lunar eclipses. Eratosthenes measured it.

The calculation rested on two convenient simplifications that were not quite exact: Syene is close to, but not precisely on, the Tropic of Cancer, and it lies slightly east of Alexandria rather than due south. Neither error was large enough to derail the result, and the fact that a calculation built on approximate assumptions and simple instruments still landed within a few percent of the true circumference is itself part of why the achievement has remained so celebrated.

name: Battle of Cynoscephalae
outcome: Roman victory; Macedonian hegemony over Greece ends

claims.text: Rome defeated Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC.
Part of the Macedonian army was caught before completing its deployment.
A flanking movement by Roman maniples attacked the phalanx from the rear.
Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks at the Isthmian Games in 196 BC.
The two armies collided unexpectedly on the "Dog's Heads" ridge in thick fog rather than by prior arrangement.
Philip V was permitted to retain his throne after the defeat, on considerably reduced terms.

summary: The Roman legion defeated the Macedonian phalanx for the first time, on broken ground in Thessaly.
significance: The first clear defeat of the Macedonian phalanx by the Roman legion, which made Rome the arbiter of Greece.
body:
Fought in 197 BC in the hills of Cynoscephalae ("Dog's Heads") in Thessaly, between the Roman army of Titus Quinctius Flamininus, with Aetolian allies, and Philip V of Macedon. It was the decisive battle of the Second Macedonian War.

Neither side planned to fight that day. The two armies, marching on either side of the same ridge in thick fog, collided by accident on rough, broken ground. Philip's right wing formed up on high ground and drove the Roman left downhill. But his left wing was still in marching column when the Romans, with war elephants, attacked it before it could deploy, and it broke.

Then an unnamed Roman tribune took about twenty maniples from the victorious Roman right and led them into the rear of Philip's successful right wing. A phalanx, packed tight with long pikes pointing forward, could not turn to face an attack from behind, and it was cut down where it stood.

Polybius drew the lesson: the phalanx was almost unbeatable head-on on level ground, but helpless once it lost that ground or its unbroken line, while the Roman maniples could adapt. Philip kept his throne but lost his fleet, his possessions in Greece and most of his army. In 196 BC Flamininus proclaimed the "freedom of the Greeks" at the Isthmian Games to huge applause — a freedom that in practice meant Roman oversight.

name: Battle of Pydna
outcome: Decisive Roman victory; Macedonian monarchy abolished

claims.text: Rome destroyed the Macedonian army at Pydna in 168 BC.
The Macedonian kingdom was abolished after the battle.
Roman maniples exploited gaps opening in the phalanx on uneven ground.
Perseus was captured and displayed in a Roman triumph.
A lunar eclipse the night before the battle was correctly predicted to Roman troops by an officer, steadying morale that the omen might otherwise have shaken.
Polybius drew on eyewitness testimony, including from Aemilius Paullus's own family, in his surviving account of the battle.

summary: Rome destroyed the Macedonian army in under an hour, abolishing the kingdom of Alexander's successors.
significance: The battle that ended the kingdom of Macedon and showed the Roman legion's superiority over the phalanx.
body:
Fought on 22 June 168 BC near Pydna, on the coast of southern Macedonia below Mount Olympus, between the Roman consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus and King Perseus of Macedon, the last of the Antigonid kings. It was the decisive battle of the Third Macedonian War.

The night before, a lunar eclipse frightened the Roman troops until the officer Gaius Sulpicius Gallus, who had predicted it, explained that it was a natural event. The next day the Macedonian phalanx advanced and at first drove the Romans back; Paullus later said that the oncoming wall of pikes was the most frightening sight of his life.

But the ground was uneven, and as the phalanx moved forward its line broke up and gaps opened. Paullus sent his flexible maniples into them. Once inside the reach of the pikes, Roman legionaries with short swords had every advantage over men holding six-metre poles in both hands. The battle was over in about an hour, with heavy Macedonian losses.

Perseus fled, was captured and was led in chains in Paullus' triumph in Rome. The Macedonian kingdom was abolished and divided into four republics; after a revolt it became a Roman province in 148 BC. Much of the detailed account comes from Polybius, who knew Paullus' family in Rome. Pydna showed the superiority of the legion over the phalanx and ended Macedon as an independent power.

name: The sack of Corinth

claims.text: Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BC after defeating the Achaean League.
The population was killed or enslaved and the city's art looted.
Carthage was destroyed by Rome in the same year.
Corinth was refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC.
The destruction of Corinth and Carthage in the same year is often treated by historians as marking Rome's definitive establishment as the dominant Mediterranean power.

summary: Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BC, killing or enslaving its population as a warning to the rest of Greece.
significance: The end of Greek independence: after 146 BC Greece was under direct Roman control.
body:
In 146 BC the Roman general Lucius Mummius captured and destroyed Corinth, the leading city of the Achaean League.

The Achaean League, provoked into a hopeless war by escalating Roman demands that it effectively dismantle itself as an independent political union, fought and lost quickly and decisively. The Roman general Lucius Mummius took Corinth, killed the adult male population, sold the surviving women and children into slavery, systematically looted the city's famous art collections, and burned what remained to the ground.

This was calculated Roman policy rather than an isolated atrocity: Rome destroyed Carthage in North Africa in the very same year, 146 BC, in an unrelated but strikingly parallel campaign. Taken together, the two destructions are often treated by later historians as the moment Rome definitively established itself as the unrivalled dominant power across the entire Mediterranean world, with both an old Greek commercial rival and an old Punic one eliminated within months of each other. The message to the rest of the Greek world in particular was unmistakable: continued resistance to Roman demands would not be met with a merely proportionate response.

Polybius, a Greek statesman who had spent seventeen years as a hostage in Rome and had grown close to prominent Roman families in that time, arrived at Corinth shortly afterward and found himself with the deeply uncomfortable task of helping organise the Roman settlement of his own newly conquered homeland. He records, with a certain dry irony, Mummius's famous indifference to the artistic value of what he was shipping back to Rome, reportedly warning the shipping contractors that if any of the looted artworks were lost in transit, they would simply have to replace them with new ones of equal quality — missing the point that many were irreplaceable originals by celebrated Greek masters.

Corinth itself lay largely empty and unrebuilt for roughly a century until Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC, repopulating it mainly with Italian freedmen rather than descendants of its original Greek inhabitants.

name: Sulla sacks Athens

claims.text: Sulla besieged and stormed Athens in 86 BC.
A destruction layer of this date is identifiable in the Athenian Agora.
Sulla felled the groves of the Academy and Lyceum for siege material.
Aristotle's library was taken to Rome as part of the plunder.
Athens had installed the philosopher-tyrant Aristion, whose harsh rule contributed to the city's desperate resistance during the siege.

summary: Sulla stormed Athens in 86 BC after it sided with Mithridates, causing damage the city never fully recovered from.
significance: The violent end of Athens' last attempt at independence, and a turning point in the city's ancient history.
body:
In 86 BC the Roman general Sulla captured and sacked Athens during the First Mithridatic War.

Athens joined Mithridates of Pontus against Rome, having suffered under Roman tax farmers. Sulla besieged the city through the winter, and the population starved — sources report people eating boiled shoe leather.

He stormed it on 1 March 86 BC. The killing in the Kerameikos was severe enough that Plutarch reports blood running through the gate. Sulla stopped the massacre, saying he spared the many for the sake of the few — a reference to Athens' past rather than its present.

He cut the sacred groves of the Academy and the Lyceum for siege timber, looted extensively, and shipped Aristotle's library to Rome. Archaeologically the destruction layer is clear across the Agora. Athens remained a revered university town but was never again politically significant.

Much of the city's suffering during the siege was blamed on Aristion, an Epicurean-trained philosopher who had made himself tyrant of Athens with Mithridates' backing and ruled harshly, executing opponents and hoarding food while ordinary citizens starved — behaviour that left the city divided and demoralised even before Sulla's final assault.

name: Battle of Actium
outcome: Decisive victory for Octavian

claims.text: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium on 2 September 31 BC.
Cleopatra's squadron left the battle and Antony followed.
Antony's land army surrendered within days.
The withdrawal was a planned breakout rather than a betrayal.
Octavian's admiral Agrippa was the tactical mastermind behind the naval blockade and victory.

summary: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra on 2 September 31 BC, effectively ending the Hellenistic age.
significance: The battle that ended the last great Hellenistic kingdom and left Octavian — soon Augustus — master of the Roman world.
body:
Fought on 2 September 31 BC off the promontory of Actium, at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf in north-western Greece, between the fleet of Octavian, commanded by Agrippa, and that of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII.

Antony and Cleopatra were blockaded in the Ambracian Gulf with a fleet weakened by malaria and desertion; Antony had already burned ships he could not crew.

He attempted a breakout. Mid-battle Cleopatra's squadron of sixty ships raised sail and ran south. Antony transferred to a lighter ship and followed, leaving his fleet and his army — which surrendered a week later.

Octavian's version, which became the official one, framed this as a foreign queen's betrayal and a Roman general's enslavement to her. A more sober reading is that the treasury and the escape were the objective and the fighting was cover. Either way, within a year both were dead and Egypt was Roman.

The victory itself owed less to Octavian personally than to his admiral Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, who had spent the preceding months systematically cutting Antony's supply lines and seizing key positions along the coast, reducing Antony's fleet to a starving, disease-ridden force well before the two sides ever engaged in open battle.

name: Death of Cleopatra and annexation of Egypt

claims.text: Cleopatra VII died in Alexandria in August 30 BC.
Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BC.
Her son Caesarion was executed.
She died from a snake bite.
Egypt was administered by an equestrian prefect accountable to Octavian, and senators needed his permission to enter; this did not make the whole province his private property.

summary: Cleopatra VII died in August 30 BC; Egypt became a Roman province, ending the last Hellenistic kingdom.
significance: The end of the last Hellenistic kingdom and of three centuries of Greek rule in Egypt.
body:
Cleopatra VII, last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, died at Alexandria in August 30 BC, a year after her and Mark Antony's defeat at Actium, as Octavian's army took the city.

Antony killed himself after a false report that Cleopatra was already dead. Cleopatra was captured alive and negotiated with Octavian's agents, but learned that he meant to parade her in his triumph in Rome. She died soon afterwards in her chambers, with her two attendants, Iras and Charmion.

Plutarch tells the famous story of an asp smuggled in a basket of figs, but admits that no one knew what really happened. Other accounts spoke of poison hidden in a hairpin; the only marks found were two faint punctures on her arm, and no snake was found in the room.

Octavian made Egypt a Roman province under a prefect of equestrian rank answerable to him, and barred senators from entering it without his permission. Egypt's grain was vital to feeding Rome, and he would not let any rival control it. Caesarion, Cleopatra's son by Julius Caesar, was hunted down and killed.

The Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by Alexander's general Ptolemy almost three centuries earlier, came to an end, and with it the last of the Hellenistic kingdoms. Historians often date the end of the Hellenistic age to this moment.

name: Decipherment of Linear B

claims.text: Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952, identifying the language as Greek.
Cretan place names provided the initial breakthrough.
Tablet PY Ta 641 provided independent confirmation.
The decipherment extended attested Greek back roughly five centuries.
Ventris circulated his working notes openly to other scholars throughout the process rather than working in isolation.

summary: Michael Ventris showed in 1952 that Linear B recorded Greek, opening five centuries of previously mute history.
significance: The decipherment that pushed written Greek back by five centuries and opened the Mycenaean world to history.
body:
In 1952 the English architect Michael Ventris showed that Linear B, the script of the Mycenaean palaces, wrote an early form of Greek.

Ventris built a grid organising the syllabic signs by shared consonant and vowel without assuming any sound values, working purely from distributional patterns in the texts.

He noticed sign-groups appearing only on Knossos tablets, likely place names, and tested Cretan toponyms against them. Amnisos, Knossos and Tulissos produced consistent values that then worked across other words.

The resulting language was Greek — an archaic form, but unmistakably Greek. Ventris had expected something related to Etruscan and initially assumed he had made an error. He announced it on BBC radio in June 1952. John Chadwick joined him, and Carl Blegen's Pylos tablet PY Ta 641, where the values produced *ti-ri-po-de* beside pictures of tripods, provided independent confirmation.

The result pushed attested Greek back 500 years before Homer and made the Mycenaean world historical rather than merely archaeological. Ventris worked in an unusually open way for a decipherment, circulating his evolving "Work Notes" to other interested scholars throughout the process rather than guarding his progress jealously, a collaborative habit that likely helped the result reach confirmation faster than it otherwise might have.

name: The Greco-Persian Wars
combatants: Greek city-states (led by Athens and Sparta)
outcome: Greek victory; Persia withdraws from the Aegean and mainland Greece

claims.text: The wars began with the Ionian Revolt in 499 BC and included two full-scale Persian invasions of mainland Greece, in 490 and 480–479 BC.
The war is traditionally held to have ended with the Peace of Callias in 449 BC, in which Persia accepted Greek autonomy in Ionia.
The Delian League, formed in 478 BC as a continuing anti-Persian alliance, grew directly out of the war's aftermath.
Herodotus' Histories, the main surviving narrative source, was written a generation after the events it describes.

After the Persian sack of 480 BC, Athenians buried damaged pre-war dedications, including sculptures like the Kritios Boy, in landfill on the Acropolis rather than reusing them, inadvertently preserving them intact for modern archaeology.

summary: Two Persian invasions of Greece, repelled at Marathon and then at Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea, that reshaped the Aegean world for a century.
significance: The wars that preserved Greek independence and launched the Athenian empire and the Classical age.
body:
The wars opened with the Ionian Revolt of 499–494 BC, a failed uprising by Greek cities on the Anatolian coast against Persian rule, in which Athens' brief involvement gave Darius I a pretext for direct action against the mainland. His 490 BC expedition was stopped at Marathon; a decade later his son Xerxes returned with a vastly larger force, winning at Thermopylae and burning Athens before losing the fleet at Salamis and, the following year, the army at Plataea, with the simultaneous naval victory at Mycale finishing Persian sea power in the Aegean.

Fighting continued at a lower intensity for another generation. Athens and its allies formed the Delian League in 478 BC explicitly to keep fighting Persia and liberate remaining Greek cities under its rule, winning a further major victory under Cimon at the Eurymedon river around 466 BC. Ancient tradition holds that the conflict was formally ended by the Peace of Callias in 449 BC, in which Persia recognised the autonomy of the Ionian Greek cities — though the treaty's existence and exact terms are disputed by modern historians, since no Greek source before the fourth century mentions it directly.

The war's most lasting consequence was institutional rather than territorial: the alliance built to fight Persia did not disband once Persia was contained, and within a generation had become the Athenian empire.

name: The Macedonian Wars
outcome: Macedon annexed as a Roman province

claims.text: Rome and Macedon fought four separate wars between 214 and 148 BC.
The Second Macedonian War ended with Flamininus's victory over Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC.
The Third Macedonian War ended with Aemilius Paullus's victory over Perseus at Pydna in 168 BC, after which the monarchy was abolished.
The Fourth Macedonian War, against the pretender Andriscus, ended with Macedon's direct annexation as a Roman province in 148 BC.
The First Macedonian War overlapped directly with Rome's war against Hannibal, reflecting Philip V's alliance with Carthage.

summary: Four wars over seven decades in which Rome dismantled the kingdom Philip II and Alexander had built, ending in direct provincial rule.
significance: The wars in which Rome conquered the kingdom of Alexander and became master of Greece.
body:
The first war (214–205 BC) grew directly out of Philip V's alliance with Hannibal against Rome during the Second Punic War, a decision that made Macedon an enemy of Rome while Rome itself was still fully consumed by the crisis of Hannibal's invasion of Italy; fought mostly through allies and proxies with minimal direct Roman involvement, it ended in an inconclusive peace that changed little on the ground. The second war (200–196 BC) was far more decisive: Flamininus defeated Philip V outright at Cynoscephalae and then proclaimed the freedom of the Greek cities at the Isthmian Games, ending Macedonian hegemony over Greece while still leaving the Macedonian kingdom itself intact, if considerably weakened, under close Roman oversight.

Philip's son Perseus inherited a weakened but still functioning state, and renewed war with Rome broke out in 171 BC. Aemilius Paullus destroyed the Macedonian army at Pydna in 168 BC in under an hour; Perseus was captured, and the monarchy — the same royal house, in unbroken line, that had produced Philip II and Alexander — was abolished outright. Macedon was split into four notionally independent republics under Roman supervision.

That arrangement lasted twenty years. When a pretender named Andriscus, claiming descent from Perseus, briefly restored the monarchy and defeated a Roman army, Rome answered with direct annexation: Macedon became a Roman province in 148 BC, ending both the war and any prospect of Macedonian independence. The Achaean War of 146 BC, which brought the destruction of Corinth, followed within two years as Rome extended the same settlement across the rest of mainland Greece.

name: Battle of Mycale
outcome: Decisive Greek victory; Persian naval power in the Aegean destroyed

claims.text: A Greek fleet under the Spartan king Leotychidas and the Athenian Xanthippus destroyed the beached Persian fleet at Cape Mycale in 479 BC.
Ancient tradition holds the battle took place on the same day as Plataea.
Ionian Greek cities revolted from Persian rule in the battle's aftermath.

summary: A Greek fleet destroyed the beached Persian navy at Mycale in 479 BC, on the same day tradition places the victory at Plataea, ending Persian sea power in the Aegean.
significance: The victory that freed the Greek cities of Ionia and turned the Persian Wars from defence into counter-attack.
body:
Fought in August 479 BC at Mycale, on the coast of Asia Minor opposite Samos, between the Greek allied fleet and the Persian navy and its land forces.

After Salamis, the remaining Persian fleet had drawn up on the beach at Mycale, opposite Samos, under the protection of a land garrison, judging open battle at sea against the Greeks too risky. The Greek fleet, initially reluctant, was persuaded by Samian envoys and Ionian Greek exiles to cross and attack anyway.

The Greeks landed and stormed the fortified camp; the Persian force, largely composed of demoralised Ionian Greek conscripts who reportedly withdrew from the fighting or actively turned on their Persian officers once the issue was in doubt, collapsed. Herodotus places the battle on the very day of Plataea, a coincidence many modern historians treat as a literary flourish rather than fact, though the two victories certainly fell close together.

Its immediate consequence was an open revolt of the Ionian Greek cities from Persian rule, which the newly formed Delian League was built specifically to protect and extend — Mycale marks the point where the defensive war became a war of liberation.

name: Battle of the Eurymedon
outcome: Decisive Delian League victory, at sea and on land in a single day

claims.text: Cimon led a Delian League fleet to victory over a Persian fleet at the mouth of the Eurymedon river, then landed and defeated Persian land forces the same day.
Around 200 Phoenician ships in Persian service were captured or destroyed.
The victory effectively ended major Persian naval activity in the Aegean for a generation.
Some ancient sources report a third engagement the same day against Persian reinforcement ships arriving from Cyprus, though this detail is less securely attested than the main battle.

summary: Cimon destroyed a Persian fleet and then its supporting army on the same day at the mouth of the Eurymedon, around 466 BC.
significance: The victory that drove Persian power from the Aegean and confirmed Athens as leader of the Delian League.
body:
Fought around 466 BC at the mouth of the Eurymedon river in Pamphylia, southern Asia Minor, between the Delian League under the Athenian Cimon and a Persian fleet and army.

Cimon caught the Persian fleet at anchor off the Pamphylian coast and destroyed or captured it before it could properly deploy, then, learning that Persian reinforcements had landed troops nearby, landed his own marines the same day and routed them too — an unusual double victory that ancient writers treated as an exceptional feat even by Athenian standards.

The scale of the win, whatever the exact numbers Plutarch and other later sources report, removed Persia as an active naval threat in the Aegean for a generation, letting the Delian League's members refocus its enormous common treasury toward Athens' own ends rather than continuous campaigning. The spoils are traditionally linked to a wave of Athenian public building in the years that followed, foreshadowing the far larger building program Pericles would launch after the mid-century peace with Persia.

Some later accounts add a third phase to the day's fighting: a squadron of Phoenician reinforcements, unaware the main battle was already lost, is said to have sailed into the same waters and been destroyed in turn by Cimon's fleet. The detail is harder to confirm independently than the main double victory, but if true it would make Eurymedon an even more thorough rout than the core tradition already describes.

name: Battle of Sphacteria
outcome: Athenian victory; Spartan hoplites surrender

claims.text: Athenian forces under Demosthenes and Cleon trapped and forced the surrender of a Spartan garrison on the island of Sphacteria in 425 BC.
Around 120 of the surrendering troops were full Spartan citizens (Spartiates), a small fraction of the total Spartan citizen body.
It was the first time Spartan hoplites had surrendered in battle rather than fighting to the death.
The captured Spartiates were held hostage at Athens and constrained Spartan strategy for years afterward.
The Athenian victory monument for the campaign is generally identified with the Nike of Paionios dedicated at Olympia.

summary: An Athenian force trapped a Spartan garrison on Sphacteria in 425 BC and forced roughly 120 Spartan citizens to surrender — an unprecedented shock to Sparta's military prestige.
significance: The first time Spartan citizen soldiers surrendered in large numbers, a shock that shook Sparta's reputation and handed Athens its best bargaining position of the war.
body:
Fought in 425 BC on the island of Sphacteria, at the entrance to the Bay of Navarino near Pylos in Messenia, between Athens and Sparta.

A largely improvised Athenian landing at Pylos, right on the Spartan mainland's own coast, left a Spartan garrison stranded on the small offshore island of Sphacteria once the Athenian fleet arrived and cut off any possibility of rescue or retreat. The subsequent siege dragged on far longer than expected in difficult terrain, until Cleon — an Athenian politician known chiefly for aggressive rhetoric rather than any military reputation, who had rashly promised the assembly a swift result largely to embarrass his political rivals — was sent out jointly with the far more experienced general Demosthenes and, against most contemporary expectations, actually delivered on his promise: the Spartan position was stormed and its survivors forced to surrender.

The surrender itself was the real historical shock, more than the tactical result. Spartan citizen-soldiers were culturally expected to die in place rather than yield under any circumstances, and the roughly 120 Spartiates taken prisoner represented a genuinely significant fraction of Sparta's entire full-citizen fighting body at a time when that population was already in long-term demographic decline and could not easily absorb such a loss. Held hostage at Athens under close guard, the prisoners gave Athens real strategic leverage for years afterward: Sparta avoided its usual annual invasions of Attica for fear of what retaliation might be visited on the captured men. The Athenian victory monument commemorating the wider campaign is generally identified by scholars with the Nike of Paionios, a soaring marble figure of Victory dedicated at Olympia and still counted among the finest surviving works of Classical Greek sculpture.

Thucydides frames the whole episode partly as an argument about the dangers and occasional successes of Athenian democratic politics — Cleon's unexpected success was resented by many contemporaries almost as much as it was celebrated, since it vindicated a brash demagogue's political gamble over the more cautious instincts of Athens's established aristocratic leadership.

name: Battle of Delium
outcome: Decisive Boeotian victory; Athenian invasion of Boeotia repelled

claims.text: A Boeotian army led by Thebes defeated an invading Athenian force at Delium in 424 BC.
Socrates served as a hoplite in the battle and was noted for his composure during the retreat.
The Theban contingent's unusually deep phalanx formation contributed to the victory.

summary: Thebes led a Boeotian army to a decisive victory over an invading Athenian force at Delium in 424 BC, in which Socrates served and reportedly distinguished himself in the retreat.
significance: A Theban victory that ended Athenian hopes of knocking Boeotia out of the Peloponnesian War, and showed the power of a deep infantry formation.
body:
Fought in 424 BC near the sanctuary of Delium on the coast of Boeotia, between an invading Athenian army and the Boeotians led by Thebes.

Athens attempted to knock Boeotia, Thebes' regional league, out of the war by seizing and fortifying the sanctuary of Delium as a forward base. A Boeotian army caught the Athenian force as it withdrew, and won decisively — one of the largest hoplite battles of the war's first phase and a serious check on Athenian ambitions on land.

Among the Athenian hoplites that day was Socrates, then in his mid-forties; Plato and other later sources describe him as remaining calm and orderly during the rout, a detail later writers used to illustrate the same self-possession he showed throughout his life, on the battlefield as much as in the agora.

The Theban infantry's notably deep formation at Delium is sometimes read by modern historians as an early ancestor of the much deeper, more radical phalanx Epaminondas would use to break Sparta at Leuctra half a century later — a continuous Theban tactical tradition of concentrating force on one flank rather than spreading it evenly along the line.

name: Battle of Mantinea (418 BC)
outcome: Decisive Spartan victory; Spartan military prestige restored

claims.text: A Spartan-led army defeated a coalition of Argos, Athens and Mantinea at Mantinea in 418 BC.
Thucydides describes it as the largest battle fought among Greek states in a very long time.
The victory restored Spartan military confidence after the humiliation of Sphacteria.
Argive democracy was briefly overthrown in the battle's aftermath and replaced with an oligarchy allied to Sparta.

summary: Sparta defeated a coalition led by Argos and Athens at Mantinea in 418 BC, restoring its military reputation after the surrender at Sphacteria.
significance: The largest land battle of the Peloponnesian War, which restored Sparta's reputation and broke the Argive alliance.
body:
Fought in 418 BC at Mantinea in Arcadia, in the central Peloponnese, between Sparta and a coalition of Argos, Mantinea and Athens.

The years after the Peace of Nicias (421 BC) were an uneasy, incomplete truce rather than real peace, and Argos assembled a coalition with Athens and Mantinea to challenge Spartan dominance of the Peloponnese while Sparta still seemed weakened by Sphacteria. The armies met at Mantinea in what Thucydides calls the largest gathering of Greek hoplites in a great many years.

Sparta's disciplined manoeuvring under King Agis II won the day, in the last major set-piece hoplite battle of the war's central phase. The defeat broke up the anti-Spartan coalition and restored confidence in Spartan arms after the shock of Sphacteria three years earlier — a psychological recovery at least as significant as the battle's immediate territorial consequences, which were modest.

The political aftershock in Argos itself was sharper than the battle's cost in the field: within months, Argive oligarchs sympathetic to Sparta overthrew the city's democracy, though the arrangement proved short-lived and democratic government was restored there before long, underlining how closely Argos's internal politics tracked its fortunes against Sparta.

name: Battle of Mantinea (362 BC)
outcome: Theban tactical victory; Epaminondas killed, Theban hegemony collapses

claims.text: Epaminondas led a Boeotian army to tactical victory over a Spartan-Athenian coalition at Mantinea in 362 BC, using the same massed-wing tactic as at Leuctra.
Epaminondas was killed at the moment of victory.
Xenophon's Hellenica ends its narrative with this battle, describing the confusion that followed as greater than before it.
Theban hegemony over Greece collapsed within a few years of Epaminondas's death.

summary: Epaminondas won again at Mantinea in 362 BC using the tactics that had broken Sparta at Leuctra — and died in the moment of victory, taking Theban hegemony down with him.
significance: The battle that ended the brief Theban supremacy in Greece, leaving no city strong enough to resist Macedon.
body:
Fought in 362 BC at Mantinea in Arcadia, in the central Peloponnese, between Thebes under Epaminondas and a coalition including Sparta and Athens.

Nine years after Leuctra, Epaminondas faced a coalition of Sparta, Athens and others determined to check continued Theban dominance of Greece. He repeated the tactic that had won at Leuctra, massing an unusually deep strike force on one wing while holding the rest of the line back, and broke the opposing formation just as decisively.

He was struck down, probably by a spear, at the height of the breakthrough. Ancient accounts describe him asking, as he lay dying, whether his shield was safe and whether the Thebans had won, and being satisfied enough by the answers to allow himself to die — a story polished by later tradition into something close to a set-piece, whether or not every detail is literal.

Xenophon's Hellenica, the main narrative source for the period, ends its account precisely here, closing with the observation that the battle left Greece in greater confusion and uncertainty than before it had been fought — a fitting epitaph for a war that changed hegemony without settling anything. Without Epaminondas, Thebes had no comparable leader, and its brief dominance of Greek affairs collapsed within a few years, leaving no power strong enough to resist the rise of Macedon under Philip II a generation later.

name: Battle of Arginusae
outcome: Athenian victory; aftermath triggers a domestic political crisis

claims.text: An Athenian fleet defeated a Spartan fleet near the Arginusae islands in 406 BC.
A storm afterward prevented the recovery of shipwrecked Athenian sailors and the dead.
The victorious generals were tried collectively and executed at Athens for the failure to rescue survivors, in a process later writers considered illegal.
Socrates, serving that year as a member of the presiding council, refused to allow the illegal collective vote to proceed.

summary: Athens won its last major naval victory of the war at Arginusae in 406 BC, then executed the victorious generals in a legally dubious mass trial over the storm-hampered rescue that followed.
significance: Athens' last great naval victory — remembered less for the battle than for the city's execution of its own winning generals.
body:
Fought in 406 BC off the Arginusae islands, between Lesbos and the coast of Asia Minor, between Athens and Sparta.

Facing a Spartan fleet with Athens' own survival at stake, an emergency Athenian force — including newly freed slaves rowing alongside citizens — won a clear victory near the Arginusae islands, off the Anatolian coast. It should have been an unqualified triumph, arguably the last real chance to recover from the war's long decline.

A storm broke immediately afterward, preventing the generals from recovering the crews of disabled ships and the bodies of the dead — a failure that was, in the circumstances, arguably unavoidable, but which the Athenian assembly treated as a capital offence. In a legally irregular move, the assembly voted to try all the generals together rather than individually as the law required; Socrates, serving that year on the presiding council (prytany), was the sole member to refuse to put the illegal motion to a vote, at real personal risk. He was overruled, and six generals were executed.

Xenophon's account presents the episode as a moment of collective madness the Athenians came to regret almost immediately afterward — and a self-inflicted wound the city, already short of experienced commanders, could not really afford so close to its final defeat.

name: Battle of Corupedium
outcome: Decisive Seleucid victory; Lysimachus killed

claims.text: Seleucus I defeated and killed Lysimachus at Corupedium in Lydia in 281 BC.
Lysimachus was the last of Alexander's original companions and successors still living at the time of the battle.
Seleucus was assassinated within months of the victory, before he could unify the territory he had just won.

summary: Seleucus killed his old comrade-in-arms Lysimachus at Corupedium in 281 BC, ending the last rivalry among Alexander's original successors.
significance: The last battle between Alexander's own generals, after which only Ptolemy's, Seleucus' and Antigonus' heirs ruled his empire.
body:
Fought in 281 BC at Corupedium in Lydia, western Asia Minor, between the aged kings Seleucus I and Lysimachus.

Lysimachus and Seleucus had fought on the same side at Ipsus twenty years earlier, but rivalry over Asia Minor and a poisonous family dispute inside Lysimachus's own court — his execution of his son Agathocles on the accusation of his wife Arsinoe had driven many of his own supporters toward Seleucus — brought the two old men to battle at Corupedium in Lydia.

Seleucus won decisively, and Lysimachus was killed in the fighting — the last of Alexander's original bodyguards and generals to die, some four decades after Alexander himself. For a brief moment, Seleucus stood as the sole survivor of that generation, master of nearly the whole of Alexander's former empire outside Egypt.

It did not last. Crossing into Europe to claim Macedon itself — the one part of Alexander's inheritance he had never held — Seleucus was assassinated within months by Ptolemy Keraunos, a disaffected son of Ptolemy I. His own son Antiochus I inherited the Seleucid heartland, while Macedon passed through a chaotic decade before settling, eventually, on Antigonus I's grandson — closing the wars of the Diadochi with the three-kingdom map that defined the Hellenistic world.

name: Siege of Rhodes
outcome: Rhodian victory; siege abandoned by negotiated settlement

claims.text: Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged Rhodes for about a year, 305–304 BC, after it refused to join Antigonid campaigns against Ptolemy.
He deployed exceptionally large siege engines, including the "Helepolis" siege tower.
Rhodes held out and negotiated a settlement preserving its independence.
The Rhodians funded the Colossus of Rhodes partly from the sale of equipment Demetrius abandoned.

summary: Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged Rhodes for a year with the largest siege engines the Greek world had seen, and failed to take it.
significance: A failed siege that made Rhodes' name — and paid for the Colossus.
body:
In 305–304 BC Demetrius Poliorcetes, son of Antigonus I, besieged the island city of Rhodes.

Rhodes had stayed on good terms with Ptolemy of Egypt, its main trading partner, and refused Antigonus's demand to join the war against him. Demetrius arrived to force the issue with a fleet and army built around siege technology on an unprecedented scale, above all the Helepolis — an armoured, multi-storey siege tower reportedly requiring thousands of men to move, packed with catapults and ballistae.

Rhodes withstood a year of assault, sabotaging engines, holding key defensive points and receiving occasional relief supplies past the blockade. Neither side could force a decision, and a negotiated peace left Rhodes formally independent while acknowledging a friendly relationship with Antigonus — a result close enough to victory for the Rhodians that they kept celebrating it for centuries.

Tradition holds that the Rhodians sold the siege equipment Demetrius left behind and used the proceeds toward a colossal bronze statue of their patron god Helios, standing some 30 metres tall near the harbour — the Colossus of Rhodes, later counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and toppled by an earthquake less than a century after it was raised.

name: Battle of Magnesia
outcome: Decisive Roman victory; Seleucid power in Anatolia ended

claims.text: A Roman-led army defeated Antiochus III's Seleucid army at Magnesia ad Sipylum in 190 BC.
The Roman general Lucius Cornelius Scipio was accompanied by his brother, Scipio Africanus, acting as a legate.
The following Treaty of Apamea (188 BC) forced the Seleucids to withdraw from Anatolia north and west of the Taurus mountains.
The kingdom of Pergamon and Rhodes gained substantial territory from the settlement.

summary: Rome broke Antiochus III's Seleucid army at Magnesia in 190 BC, ending Seleucid power west of the Taurus mountains for good.
significance: The defeat that drove the Seleucid Empire out of Asia Minor and made Rome the dominant power in the eastern Mediterranean.
body:
Fought in 190 BC near Magnesia-by-Sipylus in Lydia, western Asia Minor, between Rome under Lucius Cornelius Scipio and the Seleucid king Antiochus III.

Antiochus III, fresh from campaigns that had earned him the title "the Great" by restoring much of the Seleucid Empire's eastern territory, overreached by intervening in Greece and clashing directly with Rome. Driven out of Greece itself at Thermopylae in 191 BC, he assembled a large army — including scythed chariots and war elephants — to meet the Romans in Anatolia the following year.

At Magnesia, Roman legions and their Pergamene allies broke the Seleucid line despite being significantly outnumbered; the elephants and chariots, meant to overawe the Romans, reportedly caused as much disruption to their own side as to the enemy once panicked. The Roman commander, Lucius Cornelius Scipio, campaigned with his more famous brother Scipio Africanus, the victor over Hannibal, serving alongside him as a legate — a detail ancient sources treat as adding extra weight to the victory.

The Treaty of Apamea that followed in 188 BC was one of the most consequential settlements of the Hellenistic period: it stripped the Seleucid Empire of all territory in Anatolia north and west of the Taurus mountains, handing most of it to Rome's allies Pergamon and Rhodes, and imposed a crippling war indemnity. The Seleucid Empire never again threatened the Aegean world directly, and Rome's role as the ultimate arbiter of Hellenistic affairs was now unmistakable.

name: Alexander crosses to Troy

claims.text: Alexander crossed the Hellespont into Asia in spring 334 BC.
He visited Troy and made offerings at the traditional tomb of Achilles, his claimed ancestor.
He is said to have exchanged his own armour for relics displayed at the site as belonging to the Trojan War.

summary: Alexander opens his Persian campaign by crossing into Asia and performing rites at Troy, casting the invasion as a second Trojan War.
significance: Alexander's first act in Asia, framing the conquest of Persia as a new Trojan War with himself as the new Achilles.
body:
In spring 334 BC, Alexander ferried his invasion force across the Hellespont from Sestos to Abydos while the fleet made an unopposed crossing nearby. He is said to have thrown a spear into Asian soil from his ship and been first to land in full armour, staking a symbolic claim to the continent he had come to conquer.

He then turned aside to Troy itself, sacrificing to Athena at the citadel and laying a wreath at the tomb attributed to Achilles, the hero from whom the Argead royal house claimed descent. Ancient writers report he exchanged his own armour for relics displayed at the site as relics of the Trojan War, and ran a ceremonial race naked with his companions around the tomb in the old heroic manner.

The stop was not strategically necessary — no army opposed him here — but it did real propaganda work, framing the coming war against Persia as a second Trojan War and Alexander himself as a new Achilles, a self-comparison he is said to have cultivated for the rest of the campaign.

name: Battle of Artemisium
combatants: Greek allied fleet under Sparta and Athens
outcome: Indecisive; Greek fleet withdrew after the fall of Thermopylae

claims.text: A Greek fleet of about 270 triremes, commanded by the Spartan Eurybiades, fought Xerxes' fleet off northern Euboea in August 480 BC.
The naval fighting took place at the same time as the land battle at Thermopylae.
A storm off the coast of Magnesia destroyed a large part of the Persian fleet before the main engagements.
The Persians sent a squadron round Euboea to trap the Greeks; it was wrecked in the Hollows of Euboea.
The Greeks withdrew to Salamis after learning that Leonidas's force had been destroyed.
Herodotus gives the Persian fleet as 1,207 ships; the figure is generally regarded as inflated.

summary: A three-day naval battle off Euboea in 480 BC that held the Persian fleet while Leonidas made his stand at Thermopylae.
significance: The naval half of the Greek defence of 480 BC, which gave the allied fleet its first experience of fighting the Persians before Salamis.
body:
Fought over three days in August 480 BC off Cape Artemisium, the northern tip of Euboea, between the Greek allied fleet and the navy of Xerxes.

While Leonidas held the pass of Thermopylae, the Greek fleet gathered at Artemisium, on the northern tip of Euboea, to prevent the Persian ships from sailing down the channel behind the army. Herodotus gives 271 triremes, more than half of them Athenian, under the nominal command of the Spartan Eurybiades. The Athenian Themistocles is credited with keeping a nervous alliance in place, and, in a story Herodotus tells with some malice, with taking bribes to do so.

The Persian fleet had already lost heavily. A gale off Magnesia is said to have wrecked hundreds of ships before it arrived, and Herodotus reports a second storm that destroyed a squadron sent round the outside of Euboea to cut off the Greeks. The fighting itself lasted three days. On the first, the Greeks captured a few ships. On the second, they destroyed a Cilician squadron. On the third, the Persians attacked in force in a battle where losses were about even, but the Greek fleet was hurt worse in proportion to its size.

The outcome was indecisive. When news came that Thermopylae had fallen, the Greek admirals withdrew south, and the Persians moved on to Attica. Plutarch and some later writers described Artemisium as a victory; a better summary is that it was a delaying action that preserved the fleet.

Its importance is strategic. It showed the Greeks could stand against the Persian navy, and it set up the choice of Salamis as the place to fight.

name: Battle of Himera
combatants: Syracuse and Akragas under Gelon and Theron
outcome: Decisive Greek victory; Carthaginian army destroyed

claims.text: Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas defeated a Carthaginian army led by Hamilcar at Himera in 480 BC.
Herodotus says the battle took place on the day of Salamis; Diodorus says it took place on the day of Thermopylae.
The Carthaginians' commander Hamilcar died in the battle, though accounts of how he died differ.
Mass graves of soldiers have been excavated near ancient Himera.
The victory brought Gelon and his successors immense prestige, and Pindar's first Pythian ode joins Himera with Salamis and Plataea.
Carthaginian power in Sicily was checked for some seventy years.

summary: The Sicilian Greeks' victory over Carthage in 480 BC, by tradition on the same day as Salamis.
significance: The victory that kept Carthage out of most of Greek Sicily for seventy years and made Syracuse a great power.
body:
Fought in 480 BC at Himera on the north coast of Sicily, between the Greek tyrants Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas and a Carthaginian army under Hamilcar.

In 480 BC, while Xerxes invaded Greece, a Carthaginian expedition landed in northern Sicily. Herodotus says Carthage had been asked to attack by Terillus, the dispossessed tyrant of Himera. Diodorus gives a huge army and a fleet that came under Hamilcar's command. Gelon, tyrant of Syracuse, marched to the aid of Himera, joined by Theron of Akragas.

The battle followed a stratagem, in Diodorus's account: Gelon intercepted a letter from allies of Carthage announcing when cavalry would arrive, sent his own horsemen in their place, and struck as they entered the Carthaginian camp. Hamilcar was killed; a Carthaginian version, reported by Herodotus, says he threw himself into a sacrificial fire after his army began to lose. The Greeks burned many of the ships and took many prisoners, and Syracusan forces afterwards controlled the coast.

Greek sources tied the victory to the Persian defeat. Herodotus reports Salamis and Himera as simultaneous; Diodorus puts the battle on the day of Thermopylae. The coincidence may have been invented for the sake of symmetry, and the link reflects a sense that Greeks everywhere were fighting the same enemy. Whether there was any concerted plan between the two theatres is doubtful, and Carthage's expedition probably had its own local aims.

The site is still yielding evidence. Mass graves near Himera, excavated in recent years, held the bodies of soldiers who died there, many with battle wounds. The defeat also ended the Carthaginian ambition of conquering Sicily for a generation.

name: The Messenian Wars
outcome: Spartan conquest of Messenia; its people reduced to helots

claims.text: Sparta conquered Messenia in two wars, traditionally dated to the late 8th and 7th centuries BC.
The poet Tyrtaeus wrote war songs during the Second Messenian War.
The conquered Messenians became helots, farming the land for Spartan citizens.
Messenia was freed by Epaminondas in 369 BC.

summary: The wars in which Sparta conquered its western neighbour Messenia in the 8th and 7th centuries BC and reduced its people to helots.
