significance: The conquest that made Sparta what it was: a small citizen elite living off a huge enslaved population, and organised for war to keep it down.
body:
Messenia, the fertile south-western region of the Peloponnese west of Mount Taygetus, was conquered by its neighbour Sparta in two wars. Their history is known mainly from later and legendary sources, such as Pausanias, so the dates are traditional.

The First Messenian War, traditionally around 743–724 BC, gave Sparta control of the rich Messenian plain. The Second, traditionally around 685–668 BC, was a great revolt, led in legend by the hero Aristomenes, which Sparta crushed only after a long struggle. The Spartan poet Tyrtaeus, whose war songs survive in fragments, wrote during it, urging Spartans to stand firm in the ranks and die for their city.

The defeated Messenians became helots, a subject population bound to the land who farmed it for their Spartan masters and handed over half their harvest. This had lasting consequences. Freed from farming, Spartan citizens became full-time soldiers, and the strict system credited to Lycurgus — the agoge, common messes and constant military training — developed largely to control the helots, who greatly outnumbered them. Fear of helot revolt shaped Spartan policy for centuries; a great rising after an earthquake in 464 BC took years to suppress.

Messenia regained its freedom only in 369 BC, when Epaminondas of Thebes invaded after Leuctra and founded the new city of Messene. Without the helots, Spartan power never recovered.

name: Battle of Lade
outcome: Decisive Persian victory; end of the Ionian Revolt

claims.text: The Ionian rebels gathered 353 ships at Lade, according to Herodotus.
Most of the Samian ships deserted at the start of the battle.
Persia captured and destroyed Miletus after the battle.

summary: The naval battle off Miletus in 494 BC where the Persian fleet crushed the Ionian Greeks, ending the Ionian Revolt.
significance: The defeat that ended the Ionian Revolt and doomed Miletus, setting the stage for Persia's invasion of mainland Greece.
body:
Fought in 494 BC off the island of Lade, then a small island just offshore from Miletus in Ionia, between the fleet of the Ionian Greek cities in revolt against Persia and the Persian navy, drawn mainly from Phoenicia, Egypt, Cilicia and Cyprus.

By 494 BC the Ionian Revolt had lasted five years, and Persia was closing in on Miletus, where it had begun. The rebels decided to fight at sea. According to Herodotus they assembled 353 triremes, from Chios, Miletus, Samos, Lesbos and other cities, against some 600 Persian ships. Dionysius of Phocaea drilled the fleet hard, but after a week the crews refused to train any longer.

Meanwhile the exiled tyrants of the Ionian cities, now with the Persians, sent messages to their own peoples promising mercy if they deserted. When the battle began, most of the Samian ships sailed away, followed by the Lesbians and others. The Chians fought bravely and lost heavily, but the Ionian fleet was destroyed.

Persia then besieged and captured Miletus, killing many of its men and deporting women and children to the Persian Gulf. The revolt collapsed. Within four years Darius sent his expedition against Athens and Eretria, which had aided the rebels — the campaign that ended at Marathon.

name: The Peace of Nicias

claims.text: The Peace of Nicias was agreed between Athens and Sparta in 421 BC for a nominal fifty years.
Key terms, such as the return of Amphipolis to Athens, were never carried out.
Thucydides regarded the Peloponnesian War as one continuous war despite the peace.

summary: The treaty of 421 BC that halted the first phase of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta — an uneasy truce that soon broke down.
significance: The failed peace that divided the Peloponnesian War into two halves and led to the Sicilian Expedition.
body:
After ten years of war, both Athens and Sparta were exhausted. In 422 BC the leading hawks on each side, Cleon of Athens and Brasidas of Sparta, were both killed in battle at Amphipolis. The Athenian general Nicias then led negotiations, and in spring 421 BC the two sides agreed a peace meant to last fifty years, named after him.

Each side was to return the places and prisoners it had taken, among them the Spartan hoplites captured at Sphacteria and the Athenian colony of Amphipolis in Thrace, captured by Brasidas. But Sparta's allies Corinth, Thebes and Megara refused to accept the treaty, and the Spartan commander in Thrace refused to hand back Amphipolis. Athens and Sparta even made a separate alliance, but trust quickly evaporated.

In Athens the young Alcibiades worked against the peace. He organised an alliance of Athens with Argos, Mantinea and Elis against Sparta, which Sparta defeated at Mantinea in 418 BC. Fighting continued at the edges, Athens destroyed Melos in 416 BC, and in 415 BC it launched the Sicilian Expedition. Open war resumed in 414–413 BC.

Thucydides insisted that the "peace" was no real peace, and that the whole conflict from 431 to 404 BC was a single war.

name: The Thirty Tyrants

claims.text: After Athens' surrender in 404 BC, a Spartan-backed oligarchy of thirty men took power.
The Thirty executed some 1,500 Athenians, according to ancient sources.
Democratic exiles under Thrasybulus defeated the Thirty, and democracy was restored in 403 BC with an amnesty.

summary: The pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens by terror for about eight months after its defeat in 404 BC, until democracy was restored.
significance: The bloodiest episode in the history of Athenian politics, whose memory haunted the restored democracy — and shaped the trial of Socrates.
body:
In 404 BC, after Athens surrendered to Sparta at the end of the Peloponnesian War, the Spartan commander Lysander backed the appointment of a board of thirty Athenians to draw up new laws. Led by Critias, a relative of Plato and former associate of Socrates, they instead seized power as an oligarchy, later called the Thirty Tyrants.

With a Spartan garrison on the Acropolis, the Thirty limited citizenship to 3,000 supporters, disarmed everyone else, and carried out a reign of terror. They executed political opponents and wealthy citizens and resident foreigners whose property they wanted — some 1,500 people according to ancient sources — and drove thousands into exile. When Theramenes, a more moderate member, protested, Critias had him condemned and forced to drink hemlock.

The democratic exiles struck back. Thrasybulus seized the fortress of Phyle on the border of Attica with a small force, then occupied Piraeus. In the fighting at Mounychia, Critias was killed. Sparta, under King Pausanias, chose not to back the oligarchs to the end, and in 403 BC the democracy was restored.

The restored democracy declared an amnesty forbidding prosecutions for past political crimes, one of the first recorded amnesties in history. But the bitterness remained, and many historians think it lay behind the trial of Socrates in 399 BC, since several of his followers, Critias above all, had been among the Thirty.

name: The March of the Ten Thousand

claims.text: Some 10,000 Greek mercenaries fought for Cyrus the Younger against his brother Artaxerxes II at Cunaxa in 401 BC.
After Cyrus was killed and the Greek generals were murdered, Xenophon helped lead the army north to the Black Sea.
Reaching a mountain within sight of the sea, the soldiers shouted "Thalatta! Thalatta!" — "The sea! The sea!"
The expedition persuaded many Greeks that the Persian Empire was vulnerable.

summary: The expedition of Greek mercenaries who fought for a Persian prince at Cunaxa in 401 BC and then fought their way home from Mesopotamia to the Black Sea.
significance: An epic of survival told by Xenophon in the Anabasis, which showed the Greeks that a Greek army could march through the heart of the Persian Empire.
body:
In 401 BC Cyrus the Younger, brother of the Persian king Artaxerxes II, rebelled to seize the throne. He hired about 10,000 Greek mercenaries, many of them veterans of the Peloponnesian War, and marched from Sardis deep into Mesopotamia. At Cunaxa, near Babylon, the Greeks routed the royal troops facing them, but Cyrus charged at his brother and was killed, leaving them stranded without a cause.

The Persian satrap Tissaphernes invited the Greek generals to a parley and had them murdered. The army elected new leaders, among them the young Athenian Xenophon, a former pupil of Socrates. They decided to march north rather than back the way they had come, through the mountains of Kurdistan and Armenia in winter, fighting off the Carduchi and other peoples, suffering snow, hunger and frostbite. When the vanguard reached a mountain above the coast, Xenophon heard them shouting "Thalatta! Thalatta!" — "The sea! The sea!" They had reached the Black Sea near Trapezus (Trabzon). When the army was counted at Cerasus on the Black Sea coast, about 8,600 hoplites remained.

Xenophon told the story in his *Anabasis*, "The March Up-Country", one of the great adventure narratives of antiquity. The expedition showed that Greek hoplites could defeat Persian armies and cross the empire, an idea that encouraged later Greek plans to invade Persia — finally carried out by Alexander.

name: The Corinthian War
combatants: Thebes, Athens, Corinth and Argos, with Persian support
outcome: Ended by the King's Peace; Sparta retained leadership in Greece

claims.text: Thebes, Athens, Corinth and Argos allied against Sparta in 395 BC, backed by Persian money.
Conon, commanding a Persian fleet, destroyed the Spartan navy at Cnidus in 394 BC.
Iphicrates' light-armed peltasts destroyed a Spartan regiment near Corinth in 390 BC.

summary: The war of 395–387 BC in which Thebes, Athens, Corinth and Argos, funded by Persia, fought to break Sparta's dominance of Greece.
significance: The first great challenge to Spartan supremacy after the Peloponnesian War, which ended with Persia dictating peace to the Greeks.
body:
After defeating Athens in 404 BC, Sparta dominated Greece and began to fight Persia in Asia Minor under King Agesilaus II. Persia responded by sending money to Sparta's discontented former allies. In 395 BC Thebes, Athens, Corinth and Argos formed an alliance against Sparta; much of the fighting took place around Corinth and its Isthmus, which gave the war its name.

In 394 BC Agesilaus was recalled from Asia. The Spartans won the land battles of Nemea and Coronea that year, but at sea the exiled Athenian admiral Conon, commanding a Persian fleet, destroyed the Spartan navy off Cnidus, ending Sparta's brief naval empire. With Persian money Conon rebuilt the Long Walls of Athens. In 390 BC the Athenian general Iphicrates, using light-armed troops (peltasts), destroyed a regiment of Spartan hoplites near Corinth, a famous demonstration of what light infantry could do. Corinth and Argos briefly merged into a single state.

The war dragged on until Persia, worried by the revival of Athens, switched its support back to Sparta. In 387 BC the Spartan envoy Antalcidas and the Persian king agreed terms that all the Greeks were forced to accept — the King's Peace — which left Sparta as the dominant power in Greece.

name: The King's Peace

claims.text: The King's Peace of 387/386 BC gave the Persian king the Greek cities of Asia Minor and Cyprus.
It declared all other Greek cities autonomous, which Sparta used to break up rival leagues.
It was negotiated by the Spartan Antalcidas with the Persian king Artaxerxes II.

summary: The peace settlement of 387/386 BC, dictated by the Persian king, that ended the Corinthian War and handed the Greek cities of Asia back to Persia.
significance: A humiliating reversal of the Persian Wars: a century after Salamis, the Persian king was arbiter of Greek affairs.
body:
By 387 BC the Corinthian War had become a stalemate. The Spartan envoy Antalcidas negotiated with the Persian king Artaxerxes II, who had funded first Sparta's enemies and now, again, Sparta. The resulting terms, announced in the king's name and accepted by the Greek states at Sparta in 387/386 BC, became known as the King's Peace or the Peace of Antalcidas.

Xenophon preserves its text. The king claimed the Greek cities of Asia Minor, and Cyprus, as his own. All other Greek cities, large and small, were to be autonomous, except for three islands that remained under Athens. Anyone who refused the peace would face the king's war.

The autonomy clause served Sparta, which became the enforcer of the peace. It used it to break up alliances and federations that threatened it: the Boeotian League under Thebes was dissolved, the union of Corinth and Argos was ended, and Mantinea was split back into villages. Meanwhile the Ionian cities, freed from Persia after 479 BC, returned to Persian rule.

To many Greeks, the King's Peace was a disgrace — the Persian king now dictated terms to Greece. The resentment fed calls, voiced by Isocrates and others, for the Greeks to unite against Persia, an idea later taken up by Philip II and Alexander.

name: The Lamian War
outcome: Macedonian victory; Athenian democracy abolished

claims.text: Athens and its allies revolted against Macedon after Alexander's death in 323 BC.
The Greeks besieged Antipater in Lamia, which gave the war its name.
After the Greek defeat at Crannon in 322 BC, Antipater abolished the Athenian democracy.

summary: The revolt of Athens and other Greek states against Macedonian rule after Alexander's death, crushed in 322 BC.
significance: The last great bid for Greek independence from Macedon, whose failure ended Athenian democracy.
body:
When news of Alexander the Great's death reached Greece in 323 BC, Athens, led by the orator Hyperides and the general Leosthenes, rose against Macedonian rule. It was joined by the Aetolians, the Thessalians and other Greek states. Demosthenes, in exile, returned to support the cause.

At first the Greeks did well. Leosthenes defeated Antipater, the Macedonian regent in Europe, and besieged him in the town of Lamia in Thessaly, which gave the war its name. But Leosthenes was killed during the siege, and Macedonian reinforcements arrived from Asia under Leonnatus and then Craterus. In 322 BC the Macedonian fleet destroyed the Athenian navy off the island of Amorgos, ending Athenian sea power for good, and Antipater and Craterus defeated the Greek army at Crannon in Thessaly.

The Greek states surrendered one by one. Antipater imposed harsh terms on Athens: a Macedonian garrison was placed at Mounychia in Piraeus, and the democracy was replaced by an oligarchy in which only men with property of 2,000 drachmas or more had political rights, excluding most citizens. The leaders of the revolt were hunted down; Hyperides was executed and Demosthenes took poison on Calauria.

Athens never again held real independence, though it remained a great centre of culture.

name: The Gallic invasion of Greece

claims.text: Celtic invaders killed the Macedonian king Ptolemy Keraunos in battle in 279 BC.
A Celtic army under Brennus attacked Delphi in 279 BC and was driven off.
Antigonus II Gonatas defeated a Celtic army at Lysimachia in 277 BC and became king of Macedon.
Some of the invaders crossed into Asia Minor, where they settled as the Galatians.

summary: The invasion of Macedon and Greece by Celtic warriors in 280–279 BC, which ended at the sanctuary of Delphi.
significance: A shock that Greeks remembered as a new Persian War, which reshaped the Hellenistic kingdoms and created the Galatians of Asia Minor.
body:
In 280 BC bands of Celtic warriors, whom the Greeks called Galatai or Keltoi, moved south from the Danube into the Balkans. In 279 BC one army defeated and killed the Macedonian king Ptolemy Keraunos, leaving Macedon in chaos, and another, led by a chieftain the Greeks called Brennus, invaded Greece.

The Greeks gathered an army at Thermopylae, but, like the Persians before them, the Celts found a way round the pass. Brennus then marched on Delphi, hoping to plunder its treasures. The Aetolians and Phocians, defending the sanctuary, drove the attackers back. Later tradition said that Apollo himself saved his shrine with an earthquake, thunder and snowstorms, and the Delphians founded a festival, the Soteria, to celebrate the deliverance. Brennus was wounded and the Celtic army retreated with heavy losses.

The invasion had lasting consequences. In 277 BC Antigonus II Gonatas, son of Demetrius Poliorcetes, defeated a Celtic army at Lysimachia and won the throne of Macedon, founding the Antigonid dynasty that ruled it until 168 BC. Other Celtic groups crossed into Asia Minor, where they raided the Greek cities until they settled in central Anatolia as the Galatians. The kings of Pergamon built their prestige on victories against them, celebrated in monuments such as the Dying Gaul.

Greeks remembered the defeat of the Gauls as a defence of civilisation, like the Persian Wars.

name: The arrival of farming in Greece

claims.text: Domesticated wheat, barley, lentils, sheep and goats appear in Greece around 7000 BC.
Ancient DNA shows the first farmers of Greece were largely descended from people who came from Anatolia.
The new way of life spread from Greece and the Balkans across the rest of Europe over the following three thousand years.

summary: Around 7000 BC farmers bringing crops and herds from Anatolia settled in Greece, founding the first farming villages in Europe.
significance: The start of settled village life in Europe, and of the Greek landscape of grain, flocks and villages that lasted into modern times.
body:
Farming began in the Near East, in the "Fertile Crescent" of south-west Asia, from around 9500 BC. Around 7000 BC it reached Greece, the first part of Europe to adopt it. The plants and animals — emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils, peas, sheep and goats — had no wild ancestors in Greece, so they must have been brought from outside. Ancient DNA confirms that the first farmers were largely descended from people who came from Anatolia, though they mixed with the hunter-gatherers already living in Greece.

The newcomers settled first in the most fertile lowlands, especially the plain of Thessaly, where hundreds of village mounds are known, and in Macedonia, the Peloponnese and Crete, where Knossos was founded around 7000 BC. They built houses of mudbrick or wattle and daub, and within a few centuries were making pottery. At Franchthi Cave in the Argolid, the whole change, from hunting and fishing to farming, is recorded in a single sequence of deposits.

From Greece and the Balkans farming spread north and west, reaching Britain and Scandinavia around 4000 BC.

name: Battle of Raphia
combatants: Antiochus III of the Seleucid empire
outcome: Ptolemaic victory; southern Syria kept by Egypt

claims.text: At Raphia in 217 BC Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III and kept southern Syria.
Polybius gives about 75,000 men for Ptolemy and 68,000 for Antiochus, with African elephants facing Indian ones.
About 20,000 native Egyptians were trained and fought in the phalanx, for the first time.

summary: The great battle of 217 BC near Gaza in which Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III, with Egyptians fighting in the phalanx for the first time.
significance: One of the largest battles of the Hellenistic age; arming the Egyptians saved Ptolemaic Syria but, Polybius thought, encouraged native revolt.
body:
In the Fourth Syrian War the young Seleucid king Antiochus III invaded Ptolemaic southern Syria and Palestine. Egypt's ministers, short of Greek and Macedonian troops, took an unusual step: they trained about 20,000 native Egyptians to fight in the Macedonian phalanx.

The armies met on 22 June 217 BC near Raphia (modern Rafah), south of Gaza. Polybius, our main source, gives Ptolemy IV about 70,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and 73 African elephants, and Antiochus 62,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 102 Indian elephants. The battle was a rare clash of elephant against elephant: the smaller African forest elephants of the Ptolemies fled from the larger Indian ones. Antiochus won on his right wing and pursued too far, while in the centre the Ptolemaic phalanx, with the Egyptian contingent, broke the Seleucid infantry.

Ptolemy kept southern Syria, and the Egyptian priests celebrated the victory in a trilingual decree, the Raphia Decree. Polybius believed that the Egyptians, proud of their success, soon began to resist Greek rule, and from 206 BC a great revolt broke out in Upper Egypt.

name: Paul preaches at Athens

claims.text: According to Acts 17, Paul debated with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers at Athens and spoke before the Areopagus about an altar "to an unknown god".
He then spent eighteen months at Corinth, where he was brought before the governor Gallio.
An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's governorship to about AD 51–52, a fixed point in Paul's chronology.

summary: The visit of the apostle Paul to Athens around AD 50, when he debated philosophers in the Agora and spoke on the Areopagus.
significance: The symbolic meeting of Christianity and Greek philosophy, at the start of the Christianisation of the Greek world.
body:
Paul, a Greek-speaking Jew from Tarsus who had become a follower of Jesus, travelled through Asia Minor and Greece in the late 40s and 50s AD founding Christian communities. On his second journey, after preaching at Philippi and Thessalonica, he came to Athens around AD 50.

According to the Acts of the Apostles, he was disturbed by the city's many statues of gods. He argued in the synagogue and daily in the Agora, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers called him a "babbler" and brought him to the Areopagus, the ancient council named after the Hill of Ares. There he told them that he had seen an altar inscribed "to an unknown god", and that this god, who made the world and does not live in temples, he now proclaimed to them, quoting a Greek poet. When he spoke of the resurrection of the dead, some laughed; a few, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris, joined him.

Paul moved on to Corinth, where he stayed eighteen months, and later wrote his letters to the Corinthians. An inscription found at Delphi, naming Gallio as governor of Achaea, dates Paul's stay at Corinth to about AD 51–52. The speech is commemorated by a bronze plaque on the Areopagus.

name: Founding of the Panhellenion

claims.text: Hadrian founded the Panhellenion, a league of Greek cities with its council at Athens, in AD 131/2.
Member cities had to prove descent from old Greek mother cities.
Some thirty member cities are known from inscriptions, from mainland Greece, the islands, Asia Minor, Cyrene and Crete.

summary: Hadrian's creation, in AD 131/2, of a league of Greek cities meeting at Athens to celebrate their common Greek identity.
significance: An imperial attempt to define and honour "Greekness" itself, centred on Athens as the capital of Greek culture.
body:
In AD 131/2, during his last visit to Athens, Hadrian dedicated the temple of Olympian Zeus and founded the Panhellenion, "the council of all the Greeks". Delegates from member cities met at Athens, where they organised festivals, including new Panhellenic games, and honoured the emperor, who was worshipped as Zeus Panhellenios.

Membership was a matter of pedigree. Cities had to prove that they were truly Greek, descended from old foundations such as Athens, Sparta or Argos, and some produced elaborate genealogies to qualify. Inscriptions name about thirty members, from mainland Greece, the Aegean islands, western Asia Minor, Crete and Cyrene; the great cities of the Hellenistic east, such as Alexandria and Antioch, do not appear.

The Panhellenion had no political power: Greece was firmly governed by Rome. But it expressed the outlook of the Second Sophistic, when Greeks of the Roman empire looked back to the classical past as the source of their identity, and Athens enjoyed renewed prestige. It is last attested in the mid-3rd century AD.

name: Herulian sack of Athens

claims.text: In AD 267 the Heruli, a Germanic people raiding by sea from the Black Sea, sacked Athens.
The Athenian historian Dexippus led a force of about 2,000 men against the raiders.
Afterwards a much smaller circuit wall was built, enclosing only the area north of the Acropolis.

summary: The sack of Athens in AD 267 by the Heruli, seaborne raiders from the Black Sea, during the crisis of the Roman empire.
significance: The worst blow to Athens since Sulla; the city shrank behind a new wall and never fully regained its Roman-era splendour.
body:
In the mid-3rd century AD the Roman empire was shaken by civil wars, plague and invasions. Germanic peoples settled north of the Black Sea built fleets and raided the coasts of Asia Minor and the Aegean. In 267 a large fleet of the Heruli sailed through the Bosporus into the Aegean and sacked Athens, as well as Corinth, Argos and Sparta.

Athens had few defences. The Athenian historian Dexippus, a leading citizen, gathered about 2,000 men in the hills and harassed the raiders; fragments of his account, the *Scythica*, survive, and new pages were identified in a palimpsest in Vienna in 2014. The raiders were eventually driven off.

Archaeology shows the damage: burnt layers and destroyed buildings across the Agora, the Library of Hadrian and the Odeon of Herodes Atticus. Afterwards the Athenians built a new, much shorter wall, often called the post-Herulian wall, enclosing a small area north of the Acropolis and using stones from ruined monuments. Athens recovered as a university town, home of Neoplatonist philosophers, but the classical city had shrunk for good.

name: Dedication of Constantinople

claims.text: Constantine dedicated Constantinople on 11 May 330.
The anniversary was celebrated in the city every year for centuries.
Statues taken from Greek sanctuaries, including Delphi, adorned the new city.

summary: On 11 May 330 Constantine dedicated his new capital on the site of Byzantion: Constantinople, the New Rome.
significance: Conventionally the start of the Byzantine Empire, and the moment the centre of the Roman world moved to the Greek east.
body:
After defeating Licinius in 324 and becoming sole ruler of the Roman empire, Constantine chose Byzantion, an old Greek city on the Bosporus, as his new capital. It lay close to the dangerous Danube and Persian frontiers, on the main route between Europe and Asia, and could be supplied and defended by sea.

He enlarged the city several times over, laying out a new wall, a forum with a porphyry column topped by a statue of himself, an enlarged hippodrome, a palace, and churches. Statues and treasures were brought from all over the empire, especially from Greek cities and sanctuaries, among them the serpent column from Delphi that had commemorated the Greek victory over Persia at Plataea. Settlers were attracted with free grain and privileges, and a senate was created on the Roman model.

The city was dedicated on 11 May 330 with ceremonies that combined Christian and traditional rites. It was officially called New Rome, but soon became known after its founder as Constantinople, "the city of Constantine". Its anniversary was celebrated every year with races in the hippodrome.

name: Closure of the philosophical schools of Athens

claims.text: The chronicler John Malalas says that in 529 Justinian forbade the teaching of philosophy and law at Athens.
Damascius, head of the Neoplatonist school, and six colleagues went to the Persian court around 531, returning after a treaty guaranteed their safety.
Whether the school ended abruptly in 529 or faded more gradually is debated.

summary: In 529 Justinian banned pagans from teaching philosophy at Athens, ending the Neoplatonist school that claimed descent from Plato's Academy.
significance: Often taken as the symbolic end of ancient Greek philosophy, and of classical antiquity itself.
body:
In the 5th century Athens was still a centre of pagan philosophy. A Neoplatonist school, which saw itself as the heir of Plato's Academy, flourished under Proclus (died 485), whose house has been excavated south of the Acropolis. Its last head was Damascius.

Justinian was determined to root out paganism. In 529, the chronicler John Malalas reports, he sent a decree to Athens forbidding anyone to teach philosophy or interpret the law there. Other laws of the same years barred pagans from teaching and from public posts and confiscated their endowments.

Around 531 Damascius and six other philosophers, including Simplicius, left for Persia, hoping to find in King Khosrow I a philosopher-king. They were disappointed, and in 532 a peace treaty between Rome and Persia guaranteed that they could return and live by their beliefs. Simplicius went on writing commentaries on Aristotle, perhaps in Harran in Syria, which preserve many fragments of earlier philosophers.

Historians debate whether the school was closed by force or simply lost its funds and students. Either way, 529 has become a symbolic date for the end of the ancient world, coinciding with the founding of Benedict's monastery at Monte Cassino.

name: Byzantine Iconoclasm

claims.text: Iconoclasm — opposition to religious images — was imperial policy from the 720s or 730s to 787, and again from 815 to 843.
The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 restored the veneration of icons.
Most of what we know comes from the victorious iconophile side, which exaggerated the persecution.

summary: The long dispute, from the 720s to 843, over whether Christians might venerate images of Christ and the saints.
significance: Its outcome made icons central to Orthodox Christianity, and deepened the split between the Byzantine and western churches.
body:
By the 7th century icons — painted images of Christ, the Virgin and the saints — had become central to Byzantine devotion. In the early 8th century, after terrible defeats by the Arabs, some bishops and the emperor Leo III came to believe that God was punishing Christians for idolatry. Later tradition says that in 726 Leo removed an icon of Christ from the Chalke Gate of the palace; modern historians doubt the story and date official iconoclasm to the 730s.

His son Constantine V held a council in 754 that condemned the making and veneration of images, and monks who defended them were persecuted. In 787 the empress Irene, regent for her son, summoned the Second Council of Nicaea, which declared that icons should be venerated — though not worshipped, which belongs to God alone. Iconoclasm was revived by Leo V in 815, and finally ended in 843 when the empress Theodora, widow of Theophilos, restored the icons, an event still celebrated by the Orthodox Church as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

Most of the evidence comes from the winning side, who destroyed iconoclast writings and painted their opponents as monsters. Few religious images from before the controversy survive in the Byzantine heartlands.

name: The Great Schism of 1054

claims.text: On 16 July 1054 papal legates led by Cardinal Humbert laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Keroularios on the altar of Hagia Sophia.
The patriarch and his synod excommunicated the legates in return.
Historians now see 1054 as one stage in a gradual separation rather than a clean break; the excommunications were lifted in 1965.

summary: The mutual excommunications of 1054 between Rome and Constantinople, traditionally taken as the split between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity.
significance: The symbolic date of the division of Christianity into a Latin west and a Greek Orthodox east, which still endures.
body:
The churches of Rome and Constantinople had long been drifting apart, divided by language, by the pope's claim to authority over the whole Church, and by disputes over doctrine and practice: the western addition of *filioque* ("and the Son") to the Creed, the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, and clerical celibacy. Photius' quarrel with Rome in the 9th century had been one sharp episode.

In 1054 Pope Leo IX sent legates led by Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida to Constantinople to negotiate with the patriarch Michael Keroularios, who had closed the Latin churches in the city. The talks went badly. On 16 July 1054 Humbert walked into Hagia Sophia during the liturgy and laid a bull of excommunication against the patriarch on the altar. Keroularios and his synod responded by excommunicating the legates.

At the time few thought the breach permanent; the pope who had sent the legates had already died. The decisive estrangement came later, especially with the Crusades and the sack of Constantinople in 1204. The excommunications of 1054 were formally lifted by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras in 1965, but the churches remain separate.

name: Battle of Manzikert
outcome: Seljuk victory; emperor captured; Anatolia opened to Turkish settlement

claims.text: At Manzikert on 26 August 1071 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured the emperor Romanos IV Diogenes.
Part of the Byzantine army, under Andronikos Doukas, withdrew without fighting.
The battle itself was not a catastrophe; the civil wars that followed opened Asia Minor to Turkish conquest.

summary: The defeat of the Byzantine army by the Seljuk Turks in 1071 in eastern Anatolia, followed by the loss of most of Asia Minor.
significance: The beginning of the Turkish settlement of Anatolia, the heartland of Byzantium for centuries, and an indirect cause of the Crusades.
body:
In the 11th century the Seljuk Turks, recent converts to Islam from Central Asia, took Persia and Baghdad and began raiding the eastern provinces of the Byzantine Empire. In 1071 the emperor Romanos IV Diogenes, a soldier, marched east with a large but poorly trained army to secure the frontier in Armenia.

Near the fortress of Manzikert (modern Malazgirt, north of Lake Van) he met the sultan Alp Arslan. On 26 August, after a day of pursuing the Turkish horse archers, Romanos ordered a withdrawal to camp; the order was misunderstood, the lines broke, and the Turks attacked. The rearguard under Andronikos Doukas, a member of a rival family, withdrew without fighting. Romanos was wounded and captured. Alp Arslan treated him honourably and released him after a week in return for a ransom and a treaty.

The real disaster followed. In Constantinople the Doukas family deposed Romanos, who was blinded and died, and civil war raged for a decade. Turkish bands moved into the undefended interior of Asia Minor, and by the 1080s they had reached the Aegean coast. The emperor Alexios I Komnenos appealed to the west for help, which led to the First Crusade in 1096.

name: Sack of Constantinople (1204)

claims.text: The army of the Fourth Crusade, diverted from its goal of Egypt, stormed and sacked Constantinople in April 1204.
The bronze horses now at St Mark's in Venice were taken from the city's Hippodrome.
A Latin Empire ruled Constantinople until the Byzantines recovered it in 1261.

summary: In April 1204 the knights of the Fourth Crusade stormed Constantinople, sacked it for three days and divided the Byzantine Empire.
significance: The greatest disaster in Byzantine history; the empire never fully recovered, and the bitterness it caused poisoned relations between Greek and Latin Christians.
body:
The Fourth Crusade set out in 1202 to attack Egypt, but the crusaders could not pay the Venetians for the fleet they had ordered. They agreed to help a Byzantine prince, Alexios Angelos, regain his father's throne in return for money and troops. In 1203 they put him in power in Constantinople, but he could not pay, and was murdered by a rival. Resolved to take what they were owed, the crusaders and Venetians attacked the city from the sea walls along the Golden Horn.

On 12 April 1204 they broke in, and for three days they plundered the richest city in Christendom. Churches and palaces were looted, Hagia Sophia was stripped, and countless ancient bronze statues were melted down for coin. Relics were sent to churches across western Europe, and the Venetians carried off the four bronze horses of the Hippodrome, which still stand at St Mark's in Venice. The Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates, who fled the city, wrote a lament for it.

The crusaders crowned a Latin emperor and divided the empire among themselves; Venice took key islands and ports. Byzantine successor states survived at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond, and in 1261 the emperor of Nicaea, Michael VIII Palaiologos, recovered Constantinople.

name: Fall of Constantinople
combatants: Constantine XI Palaiologos (Byzantines, Genoese and Venetians)
outcome: Ottoman conquest; end of the Byzantine Empire

claims.text: Mehmed II's army besieged Constantinople from 6 April 1453 and took it by storm on 29 May.
The defenders numbered about 7,000; estimates of the Ottoman army vary widely, but most historians suggest 50,000–80,000 fighting men.
Ottoman cannon, including great bombards cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban, battered breaches in the Theodosian Walls.

summary: On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople after a siege of 53 days, ending the Byzantine Empire.
significance: The end of the Roman empire in the east after nearly fifteen centuries, and a turning point between the Middle Ages and the modern world.
body:
By 1453 the Byzantine Empire was reduced to Constantinople and a few territories in Greece, surrounded by the Ottoman state. The young sultan Mehmed II, aged twenty-one, was determined to take the city. He built a fortress on the Bosporus to cut it off, and gathered a huge army and artillery, including giant bombards cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban.

The siege began on 6 April. The defenders — Greeks, with Genoese and Venetian volunteers — numbered only about 7,000 to hold 22 kilometres of walls. For weeks the cannon pounded the land walls, while the defenders repaired the breaches by night. A great chain kept the Ottoman fleet out of the Golden Horn, until on 22 April Mehmed had about seventy ships dragged over the hill behind Galata on greased logs and launched them into the harbour.

Before dawn on 29 May the Ottomans launched a final assault. After hours of fighting, the Genoese commander Giustiniani was wounded and carried away, his men faltered, and Janissaries broke through near the Gate of St Romanus. The emperor Constantine XI died in the fighting. The city was sacked; that day Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia and had it turned into a mosque. Constantinople became the Ottoman capital. Mystras fell in 1460 and Trebizond, the last Byzantine state, in 1461.

name: Removal of the Parthenon Marbles

claims.text: Between 1801 and about 1812 agents of Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, removed about half the surviving sculpture of the Parthenon.
Elgin claimed Ottoman permission in a firman of 1801, which survives only in an Italian translation; whether it authorised removal is disputed.
The British government bought the collection in 1816 for £35,000 and placed it in the British Museum.

summary: The removal of much of the Parthenon's sculpture by Lord Elgin's agents in 1801–1812, now in the British Museum.
significance: It brought classical Greek sculpture to the eyes of western Europe, and began the longest-running dispute over the return of cultural heritage.
body:
Thomas Bruce, seventh Earl of Elgin, became British ambassador to the Ottoman sultan in 1799. He first planned to have drawings and casts made of the monuments of Athens, then under Ottoman rule. In 1801 he obtained a document (*firman*) from the Ottoman government; it survives only in an Italian translation, and whether it permitted the removal of sculptures from the buildings, rather than from the ground, is still disputed.

Elgin's agents, led by the painter Giovanni Battista Lusieri, removed about half of the surviving sculptures of the Parthenon — some 75 metres of the frieze, 15 metopes and 17 pediment figures — as well as a caryatid from the Erechtheion and parts of the temple of Athena Nike. Some pieces were sawn off the buildings. One ship, the *Mentor*, sank off Kythera in 1802, and its cargo was raised by divers. The last shipments reached Britain in 1812.

The poet Byron attacked Elgin as a vandal. Elgin, deep in debt, sold the collection to the British government, which after an inquiry by Parliament bought it in 1816 for £35,000. The marbles, displayed in the British Museum, transformed European ideas of Greek art. Greece formally requested their return in 1983, and the new Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009, has a gallery waiting for them.

name: Decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs

claims.text: Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in his Lettre à M. Dacier, read in Paris on 27 September 1822.
The Greek text of the Rosetta Stone, with the names of Ptolemy and Cleopatra in cartouches, provided the key.
Thomas Young had earlier made important progress, and the credit was bitterly disputed.

summary: In 1822 Champollion showed how to read Egyptian hieroglyphs, using the Greek text of the Rosetta Stone as his key.
significance: It opened three thousand years of Egyptian history, and showed how a Greek translation could unlock a lost script.
body:
The Rosetta Stone, found by French soldiers in 1799, carried the same decree of 196 BC in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Scholars could read the Greek, which honoured Ptolemy V, and so knew what the Egyptian texts said; the problem was how the scripts worked. Many believed hieroglyphs were purely symbolic pictures.

The English polymath Thomas Young recognised that the oval rings (cartouches) contained royal names, and identified some signs in the name of Ptolemy. The French scholar Jean-François Champollion, who had studied Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language, went further. Comparing the cartouche of Ptolemy on the Rosetta Stone with that of Cleopatra on an obelisk from Philae, he worked out the sound values of several signs, and then read the names of other rulers, including the pharaohs Ramesses and Thutmose — proving that the script was used for Egyptian names, not just Greek ones.

On 27 September 1822 he presented his results in a letter to Bon-Joseph Dacier, secretary of the Académie des Inscriptions in Paris. In his *Précis* of 1824 he showed that hieroglyphs combined sound-signs and meaning-signs. Young and Champollion's supporters long disputed the credit. Later trilingual decrees such as the Canopus Decree confirmed his system.

name: Greek War of Independence

claims.text: The revolt against Ottoman rule broke out in the spring of 1821; 25 March is celebrated as Independence Day.
British, French and Russian fleets destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino in 1827.
The London Protocol of 1830 recognised Greece as an independent state.

summary: The war of 1821–1830 in which the Greeks won independence from the Ottoman Empire, with the help of European volunteers and powers.
significance: It created the modern Greek state, inspired by the memory of both ancient Greece and Byzantium, and made Athens its capital.
body:
After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 most Greeks lived under Ottoman rule for nearly four centuries. In the late 18th century a merchant class, the Enlightenment and the example of the French Revolution fed a movement for freedom, and a secret society, the Philiki Etaireia, prepared a revolt.

In February 1821 Alexandros Ypsilantis led a rising in the Danubian principalities, which failed, and in March the Peloponnese rose; 25 March, the Feast of the Annunciation, became the national day. The Greeks took Tripolitsa in the autumn, with a massacre of its Muslim inhabitants, and the Ottomans answered with the massacre of Chios in 1822, painted by Delacroix. The Acropolis was besieged by both sides; legend says the Greeks sent the Ottoman garrison lead to stop them melting the Parthenon's clamps for bullets.

European philhellenes, steeped in classical education, came to fight; the poet Byron died of fever at Missolonghi in 1824. When an Egyptian army under Ibrahim Pasha was close to crushing the revolt, Britain, France and Russia intervened, destroying the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino in 1827. The London Protocol of 1830 recognised an independent Greece. A Bavarian prince became King Otto, and in 1834 Athens, then a small town, was made the capital; the Acropolis was cleared of its later buildings.

name: The Great Excavation of Delphi

claims.text: The French School at Athens excavated the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi from 1892 to 1903 under Théophile Homolle.
The village of Kastri, built over the sanctuary, was moved to a new site to make the dig possible.
The finds included the bronze Charioteer in 1896 and hymns to Apollo inscribed with musical notation.

summary: The French excavation of the sanctuary of Delphi in 1892–1903, for which a whole village was moved.
significance: It uncovered the most famous oracle of antiquity, with the Charioteer and the treasuries of the Sacred Way.
body:
For centuries the site of the Delphic sanctuary lay buried under the village of Kastri, whose houses stood on top of the ruins. Travellers from the 17th century on recognised inscriptions and walls, but systematic excavation was impossible while the village stood.

In 1891, after long negotiations — linked, it was said, to a trade agreement on Greek currants — the Greek government granted France the right to excavate, and the villagers were rehoused at a new site to the west, the modern village of Delphi. From 1892 to 1903 the French School at Athens under Théophile Homolle carried out what became known as the "Great Excavation", employing hundreds of workers and a light railway to remove the earth.

They uncovered the temple of Apollo, the theatre, the stadium, the Sacred Way with its treasuries, and thousands of inscriptions, using Pausanias' description as their guide. Among the finds were the twin kouroi known as Kleobis and Biton, the bronze Charioteer, found in 1896, and two hymns to Apollo of the 2nd century BC with musical notation, which were performed again in Paris. The Athenian Treasury was rebuilt from its own blocks in 1903–06. Excavation and study have continued ever since.

name: First modern Olympic Games

claims.text: The first modern Olympic Games, organised by Pierre de Coubertin's International Olympic Committee, were held in Athens on 6–15 April 1896.
The main venue was the Panathenaic Stadium, rebuilt in marble with money from Georgios Averoff on the site of Herodes Atticus' stadium.
The Greek water-carrier Spyridon Louis won the first marathon race.

summary: The first modern Olympic Games, held in Athens in April 1896 in the rebuilt Panathenaic Stadium.
significance: The revival of the ancient Games as the world's greatest sporting festival, staged in Greece as a tribute to its classical past.
body:
The excavation of Olympia by German archaeologists from 1875 revived interest in the ancient Games. In Greece a wealthy patriot, Evangelos Zappas, had already funded national "Olympics" in Athens in 1859, 1870 and 1875. In 1894 the French educator Pierre de Coubertin, who believed in sport as a moral education, held a congress at the Sorbonne that founded the International Olympic Committee, with the Greek writer Demetrios Vikelas as its first president, and chose Athens to host the first Games.

The Panathenaic Stadium, built in marble by Herodes Atticus in the 2nd century AD, was excavated and rebuilt in white marble with money from the merchant Georgios Averoff. The Games were held on 6–15 April 1896, with about 240 athletes, all men, from some fourteen countries, competing in athletics, wrestling, gymnastics, cycling, fencing, shooting, swimming and tennis. The American James Connolly won the first event, the triple jump.

The French scholar Michel Bréal proposed a new race from Marathon to Athens, inspired by the legend of the messenger who announced the victory of 490 BC. It was won by the Greek water-carrier Spyridon Louis, to the delight of the home crowd, and became the symbolic event of the modern Games.

name: Draco's laws

claims.text: Draco is said to have issued the first written laws of Athens in about 621/620 BC.
A later inscription of 409/408 BC republishes his law on homicide, distinguishing deliberate from accidental killing.
Solon repealed all of Draco's laws except those on homicide.
The harshness that gave the word 'draconian' to English comes from later tradition that his penalty for most offences was death.

milestones.text: The homicide law of Draco is cut again on stone in the Athenian Agora.

summary: The first written code of Athenian law, drawn up about 621 BC, remembered for its severity and for the homicide law that survived Solon's reforms.
significance: The beginning of written law in Athens and an early step in separating punishment from private revenge.
body:
Around 621/620 BC, the Athenians appointed Draco to write down their laws. Before that, officials interpreted unwritten custom, usually in favour of the aristocracy. Draco's laws, were reported by later writers to have made death the penalty for almost every offence, so that they were 'written in blood'. Since most of the evidence is late, how many of the laws covered more than killing is uncertain.

The homicide law is the best documented part. A copy cut in stone in 409/408 BC, found in the Agora, restates it and shows it distinguished intentional killing from accidental and justified killing, and specified who could prosecute and when a killer might be accepted back into the community after exile. It set up the Ephetai, a panel of judges, to hear cases, thereby moving blood-feud out of private hands.

Solon repealed Draco's other laws in 594/593 BC, but the homicide law remained in force for centuries.

name: Cylon's coup

claims.text: The Olympic victor Cylon tried to make himself tyrant of Athens by seizing the Acropolis, probably around 632 BC.
Cylon was supported by troops from Megara, where his father-in-law Theagenes was tyrant.
The conspirators who took refuge at the altar of Athena were killed after being lured out under a promise of safety.
The killing brought a curse on the Alcmaeonid family, and they were later exiled in the time of Solon.

summary: A failed attempt by the Olympic victor Cylon to seize power in Athens around 632 BC, whose bloody end left a curse on the city.
significance: One of the earliest datable events of Athenian history, and the origin of a hereditary curse that shaped Athenian politics for generations.
body:
Cylon, an Athenian noble and winner at the Olympics, married the daughter of Theagenes, tyrant of Megara. Encouraged by an oracle from Delphi, which told him to take the Acropolis during a festival of Zeus, he seized the citadel with a small force and some Megarian troops. The Athenians gathered in the country to besiege it.

Cylon and his brother escaped, while the rest, starving, took refuge at the altar of Athena. The chief magistrate, Megacles of the Alcmaeonid family, persuaded them to leave under a promise of safety, but some of them were killed on the way, including some at the altar of the Eumenides. Thucydides says the guilty were thereafter regarded as cursed.

The curse was revived in political quarrels. The Alcmaeonids were tried and exiled about 600 BC, and the Cretan holy man Epimenides came to purify the city. Their descendants, including Cleisthenes and Pericles, were taunted with the old stain by their enemies, down to Sparta's demand in 432 BC.

name: Introduction of ostracism

claims.text: Ostracism was an annual vote in which Athenians could exile a citizen for ten years without trial by writing his name on a potsherd.
Ancient sources attribute the law to Cleisthenes, but the first known ostracism took place in 487 BC.
At least 6,000 votes were needed, and thousands of inscribed ostraka have been found in the Agora and the Kerameikos.
The last known ostracism was that of Hyperbolus around 416 BC.

milestones.text: Over a hundred ostraka against Themistocles are found in a well on the north slope of the Acropolis.

summary: The Athenian practice of banishing a citizen for ten years by a vote scratched on potsherds, introduced after Cleisthenes' reforms and used from 487 BC.
significance: A distinctive device of Athenian democracy, intended to control powerful men without killing or trying them.
body:
Each year, in the sixth prytany, the Athenian Assembly was asked whether an ostracism should be held. If it voted yes, then two months later citizens wrote the name of a man they wished to see exiled on a fragment of pottery (*ostrakon*) and left it at the Agora. If at least 6,000 votes were cast, the man named most often had to leave Attica for ten years, though he did not lose his property or citizenship.

Ancient writers link the law to Cleisthenes, but it was not used until 487 BC, when Hipparchus, son of Charmus, a relative of the Peisistratids, was banished. Later targets included Aristides, Themistocles, Cimon and Thucydides son of Melesias. About 416 BC the Assembly used the procedure against Hyperbolus, a demagogue, and it fell out of use afterwards.

Thousands of ostraka have been found, in the Agora and at other sites, and these show how voters spelt names and abused their targets. Some are inscribed by the same hand, which suggests that the voting was organised. Modern scholars debate whether ostracism was meant to prevent tyranny or to resolve political deadlock.
